lessons.title: Know what a row represents

lead.text: Back to the notebook by the till. It works because every line means the same kind of thing: a line is a cup, and each line records the same facts about it, which are the day, the customer and the price. If the barista wrote a line for each cup on Monday and a line for each customer on Tuesday, nobody could add the pages up.

A database keeps its information in tables, and a table is the notebook page laid out as a grid. Each line becomes a row, and each fact becomes a column. A small shop might record its customers like this.

afterFigure.text: Each row in the grid is one customer. Ada, Ben, Cy and Dee have a row apiece, and every row carries the same three facts, which are the columns id, name and region. The code above the grid is a request to see those columns. Later lessons explain how to write requests like that, and for now it only matters what comes back.

Counting rows means counting the thing the table is about. If the café's notebook has one row per cup, a day's page holds as many rows as cups were sold, and the number of customers is a separate count. Every row also needs a name of its own, which is where we go next.

queries.label: Customers
queries.sql: SELECT id, name, region FROM customers ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Names only
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The café notebook has one line for every cup sold.

A row needs a name, because two rows can hold the same facts. Suppose a school keeps a list of its students, and two of them are both called Sam. If the only way to refer to a student were by name, nobody could say which Sam they meant.

The fix is a column that holds a different value in every row. A school would give each student a number and record it in a column called id. A column like that is called a primary key, because it names each row exactly once. In the shop's tables the primary key is always the column called id, so Ada is customer 1 and Ben is customer 2 whatever else about them changes.

Most columns are allowed to repeat. Two customers can live in the same region and the table is no worse for it. Only the key has to differ from row to row, and that matters in a moment, when a second table needs a way to point at a row of the first.
Names can repeat, so a table needs something else to tell its rows apart.

The shop now sells things, and a customer can place any number of orders. Writing every order into the customers table would repeat Ada's name and region each time, and the table would stop being about customers. So the shop starts a second table with one row for each order.

Here it is, with the customers beside it. Each order has an id of its own, from 101 to 106, and that id is the primary key of the orders table. The table also has to say whose order it was, and it does that with a column called customer_id, which holds the id of a row in customers.

afterFigure.text: Because one customer can place several orders, the same customer_id can turn up in more than one row of orders. Ada is customer 1, and her number can sit on any order she placed. That is allowed, because customer_id doesn't name the order. The order's own id does that.

So a column that holds another table's key can repeat, while a primary key can't. Following a customer through the shop means reading customer_id, and counting orders means counting rows of the orders table.

queries.label: Orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, item, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Customers
queries.sql: SELECT id, name, region FROM customers ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Each row of each table stands for one thing, and the id column names it.

queries.label: Ids and names
queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Ids and references
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The orders.customer_id column stores the id of the customer who placed each order.

queries.label: Ada's orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Ben's orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 2 ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: When a value is not known

lead.text: Order 106 was taken by phone. The customer confirmed the item, but nobody has agreed the price yet. The amount cell still has to hold something, and the obvious choice is 0. That would claim the order cost nothing, and every total of the amounts would then be wrong without anyone noticing.

Databases have a marker for exactly this situation. It is called NULL, and it means that there is no value in this cell because the value isn't known. NULL stands for the absence of a fact, which makes it a different thing from zero and from an empty piece of text. The picture shows where it sits in the orders table.

afterFigure.text: The difference matters most when you count or add. A total over the amounts should skip order 106, because no amount is recorded for it, instead of treating it as a free order. A later lesson shows exactly how a total deals with NULL. For now the point is that the table says honestly what it doesn't know.

queries.label: Unknown amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Order 106 has no agreed price yet, so its amount cell has to say so.
Last, the shop gets another customer. Elm signs up today and hasn't ordered anything yet.

Think about which tables change. Elm is a new customer, so customers gains a row with the next free id. Elm has bought nothing, so orders is left exactly as it was. The two tables count different things, and each count follows the rows of its own table.

That is why a shop can have a different number of customers and orders, and why neither number says anything about the other. Whenever you count rows, first ask what one row of that table stands for, and count that.
The shop's customers table holds Ada, Ben, Cy and Dee.

lessons.orientation: Identify the thing each table row represents and keep missing values distinct from zero.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A café keeps a notebook by the till. Every time someone buys a cup, the barista writes one line: the day, who bought it and what it cost. By Monday evening the page is full of short lines, and nobody has counted anything yet.

On Monday Mia bought three cups and Sam bought two. The owner wants to know how much was sold, and a few days later wants to know who comes in most often. Both answers are on the page, yet they come from counting different things. One counts cups and the other counts people.

Databases face the same choice all the time, and they store their information in much the same way as the notebook. This lesson follows a small shop's records as they grow. It starts with what one line stands for and how each line gets a name of its own, then asks what to write down when a fact isn't known.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say what one row stands for, and keep an unknown value apart from zero.

recap.keyIdea: A row stands for one thing and its primary key names it, so count rows by that thing, and record a missing value as NULL, never as 0.

blocks.text: Back at the notebook, the count followed the thing a line stands for. You counted 5 lines for Monday's cups, 2 order rows for customer 1 and 5 customers once Elm joined, and you gave an unknown price a marker of its own instead of writing 0.

recap.nextHook: The shop's orders table has six columns, and most questions need only two or three of them. The next lesson starts with a colleague who asks for exactly that: a short version of the table, with nothing deleted from the original.

lessons.title: Choose the columns you need

lead.text: The shop's orders table has six columns, and most questions about it need only a few of them. Asking a database for something is called writing a query, and the simplest query has two parts. SELECT lists the columns you want, separated by commas. FROM names the table to read them from.

So SELECT id, item FROM orders asks for the id and the item of every order, and nothing else. The answer is a new, smaller grid called the result, built at the moment you ask. Use the buttons under the picture to compare asking for everything with asking for two columns.

afterFigure.text: A star in place of the list means every column, so SELECT * FROM orders gives the whole table back. The result has the same six rows either way. SELECT decides which columns appear, and the rows come along unchanged.

queries.label: Every column
queries.sql: SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Id and item
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Each name in the list after SELECT becomes one column of the result.

Think back to the colleague's request. Hiding the columns left your own sheet complete, and a query treats a table the same way. It reads the stored table and builds a separate result from it. Whatever you ask for, the table behind the result keeps all of its columns and all of its rows.

That is what makes asking safe. One person can ask for two columns while another asks for five, and neither changes what the other sees. If you leave out a column you turn out to need, you ask again with a longer list, because the column was never gone.
The result is a copy built for one question, so you can reshape it as much as you like. The next two screens do exactly that, first by changing a heading and then by working out a new column.
Hiding a column in a shared view takes it out of the view only.

The columns of a result normally carry the table's own names, but those names aren't always the ones a reader wants. Your colleague might call the amount column price. You can ask for that by writing AS after the column, as in SELECT id, amount AS price FROM orders. The word after AS is an alias, a name that column goes by in this result.
Compare the two queries in the picture. They return the same ids and the same numbers, and the second one labels its second column price.

afterFigure.text: Only the heading in the result changes. Every amount is the same as before, and the table still calls its column amount, so the next query can use that name again. An alias is a label on the copy you were handed, and nothing stored is renamed.

queries.label: Without AS
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: With AS
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount AS price FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The query SELECT id, amount AS price FROM orders adds an alias.

steps.headline: A column worked out from others

lead.text: A column in the result doesn't have to be copied straight from the table. After SELECT you can write an expression, which is a small calculation made from a row's own values. Take amount / 2, for example. The database works it out separately for each row and puts the answers in the result, and AS gives the new column a heading, as in amount / 2 AS half.

An unknown value stays unknown. Half of a missing amount is still missing, so a NULL goes in and a NULL comes out. The picture sets the original amounts beside the halved ones, and order 106 shows it.

afterFigure.text: The expression uses the usual signs for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing, which are +, −, * and /. Changing the expression changes the question the result answers. Halving scales every amount, while adding ten shifts every amount by the same sum. Each answer comes from that row's own values, and the stored table is never touched.

queries.label: Original amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Halve each amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount / 2 AS half FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A SELECT list can hold an expression, and it is worked out once for every row.
Changing the expression changes the question. Doubling scales each amount, and this query adds a fixed sum instead.

lessons.orientation: Use SELECT and aliases to shape a result without changing the stored table.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A colleague asks for the shop's orders, so you open the spreadsheet. It has six columns of facts about each order, and your colleague only wants to compare prices. You hide every column except three and send them that view.

Nothing has been deleted. Your colleague sees three columns, and your own sheet still has all six, ready for the next person who wants something different. People reshape a sheet like this all the time before they share it. They hide columns, give a column a friendlier heading, or add a column that works something out from the others.

A database does the same when you ask it for a new view of a table. This lesson takes the shop's orders table through each of those changes in turn. The table itself never changes, and every answer is a fresh result built next to it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll shape a query result with SELECT, AS and simple expressions, knowing the stored table never changes.

recap.keyIdea: SELECT shapes the result with the columns and expressions you list. AS labels them, and the stored table stays exactly as it was.

blocks.text: Back with your colleague's request, you counted 2 result columns, saw that hiding columns leaves all 6 in the sheet, and worked out 160 for a doubled amount of 80 and 30 for 10 added to 20. The orders table never changed.

recap.nextHook: Every query so far has returned all six orders, whatever columns it showed. A bookshop sign that covers only some of the books on the shelf begins the following lesson, which is about keeping just the rows that pass a test.

lessons.title: Write the condition you mean

steps.headline: A test that each row passes or fails

lead.text: Take a shop sign that says 'Under £10'. It is a test you can apply to any book, and every book either passes or fails it. A book priced at exactly 10 pounds fails, because 10 is not under 10. A test like that is called a condition.

In a query the condition goes after WHERE, and the database keeps the rows that pass it and drops the rest. WHERE amount > 50 keeps the orders worth more than 50. The comparison signs are = for equal, <> for not equal, > and < for greater and less, and >= and <= for greater or equal and less or equal. The two signs with an equals sign include the line itself. The picture sets two of them side by side.

afterFigure.text: Both queries read the same orders. The first keeps the two orders worth exactly 20, and the second drops them because 20 is not more than 20. Which sign you want depends on the sentence in your head. 'At least' and 'at most' include the line, while 'more than' and 'less than' leave it out.

queries.label: At least 20
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 20 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: More than 20
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 20 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Each book on the shelf either passes the sign's test or fails it.

One order in the shop has no amount at all. Order 106 holds NULL, and a test on an unknown value can't come out true, because the database has no way to show that an unknown number is above or below anything. WHERE keeps only the rows whose condition is true, so a row with a missing amount is dropped by every test on that amount, including tests such as amount <= 40 that look as if it might survive.

To find the missing amounts themselves you need a different test. amount = NULL doesn't work, because nothing is ever equal to an unknown value, not even another unknown one. SQL has its own wording for this: amount IS NULL keeps the rows whose amount is missing, and amount IS NOT NULL keeps the rest.

afterFigure.text: Look for order 106 in the picture. It is missing from the first result, and it appears only when the condition asks for a missing amount directly.

queries.label: Amount at most 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount <= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Missing amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Amount known
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Of the six orders, one has no known amount.

queries.label: At least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: At least 80
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 80 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A shop owner rarely wants a single test. She might want the orders that are paid and also worth at least 40, or the orders that are paid or worth at least 40. Two conditions can be joined into one rule with AND and OR. With AND a row has to pass both tests, and with OR a row has to pass at least one of them.

That makes AND the stricter word. Adding a test with AND can only remove rows, because each row has more to satisfy, while adding a test with OR can only let more rows in. A missing amount still can't pass the amount test, so a row with one survives an OR only by passing the other test.

afterFigure.text: Order 106 shows the difference in the picture. It is a Lamp with no known amount, so it fails the AND query. It appears in the OR query, because it passes the item test.

queries.label: Lamp AND at least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, item, amount FROM orders WHERE item = 'Lamp' AND amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Lamp OR at least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, item, amount FROM orders WHERE item = 'Lamp' OR amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A row must pass every test that AND joins.

queries.label: Both conditions
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Either condition
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' OR amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: With OR, a row stays when either test is true.

steps.headline: On the line and between lines

lead.text: Back to the line itself. A range such as 'from 20 to 40' has two ends, and the question is whether the ends count. BETWEEN 20 AND 40 includes both of them, so it means the same as amount >= 20 AND amount <= 40. Writing amount > 20 AND amount < 40 leaves both ends out.

Say the rule aloud before you write it. 'From 20 to 40' and 'between 20 and 40' usually mean that the ends count, while 'over 20 and under 40' means they don't. The comparison signs are the exact version of that wording. The picture runs both versions over the shop's orders.

afterFigure.text: As before, an order with a missing amount passes neither query. The ends matter whenever a value can land exactly on one, and in the shop several amounts do.

queries.label: Ends counted
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount BETWEEN 20 AND 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Ends left out
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 20 AND amount < 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Compare a range that counts its ends with one that leaves them out.

Sometimes the condition isn't a range. The shop might want the orders for Books or Lamps. One way is item = 'Book' OR item = 'Lamp'. A shorter way is IN, which keeps a row whose value matches anything in a list, as in item IN ('Book', 'Lamp'). Text goes inside single quotes.
The picture shows two lists run over the same orders.

afterFigure.text: This condition looks at the item, so the unknown amount on order 106 makes no difference to it. The order is a Lamp, and it passes. Conditions on different columns don't affect each other, which is why a missing amount matters only to tests that read the amount.

queries.label: Book or Lamp
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item IN ('Book', 'Lamp') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Desk or Lamp
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item IN ('Desk', 'Lamp') ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A list of accepted values is another kind of condition.

queries.label: Book or Lamp
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item IN ('Book', 'Lamp') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Missing amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Use SQL conditions to select exactly the rows your question requires.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A bookshop puts a sign on one shelf. It says 'Books at least £20', and the shelf holds books priced at 5, 12, 20, 25 and 30 pounds. A customer reads the sign and works out which of the books it covers.

The sign is a test, and each book either passes it or doesn't. Most books are clear. The book at exactly 20 pounds is the one that needs a moment's thought, because it sits on the line that the test draws.

A query carries tests like this, and it can apply one to a table of many thousands of orders as easily as to a shelf of five books. This lesson shows how to write the test you mean. The hard cases are the value that sits exactly on the line and the order whose price nobody knows. It also shows how to join two tests into one rule.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write conditions that keep exactly the rows you mean, including at the boundary and for unknown values.

recap.keyIdea: WHERE keeps the rows whose condition is true. Choose the comparison, the boundary and AND or OR for exactly the rows you mean.

blocks.text: Back at the shelf, the sign's test became a condition you could write. You counted 3 orders of at least 40 and 2 that were paid and large, and you saw that an order with an unknown amount passed no comparison.

recap.nextHook: A condition decides which rows stay, and it says nothing about their order. Five runners and a stopwatch begin the next lesson, because a medal depends on who finished first.

lessons.title: Make the first row meaningful

lead.text: A table hands back its rows in whatever order suits the database, and nothing promises that the order stays the same from one query to the next. If the order matters, the query has to ask for it. ORDER BY names the column to sort on, and each sort runs one of two ways. ASC puts the smallest value first, and DESC puts the largest first.

So ORDER BY amount DESC puts the biggest orders at the top, and ORDER BY id ASC lists the orders from the lowest id upwards. Without an ORDER BY the words 'first' and 'last' mean nothing, because the rows have no promised order. The picture lists the same six orders both ways.

afterFigure.text: The two results hold exactly the same rows, and only the order differs. It differs because the query asked. ORDER BY is the one part of a query that promises an order, and the way the table is stored or the way the columns are listed promises nothing.

queries.label: Order A
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Order B
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC;

lead.text: The same six orders can come back in different orders.

Sorting is the first half of the timekeeper's job. The second half is the line under the third name, and in a query that line is LIMIT. LIMIT 3 keeps the first three rows of the result and drops the rest, so ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 3 means 'put the largest first, then keep three'.

The order of those two steps is built in. The database sorts first and cuts afterwards, which is why a limit on its own finds nothing useful: the first three rows of an unsorted result could be any three. The picture takes the known amounts smallest first and keeps two of them, and then four.

afterFigure.text: A limit is a ceiling and not a target. LIMIT 10 over a result of only two rows returns those two rows, because the query can't add rows that were never there.

queries.label: Two smallest
queries.sql: SELECT amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC LIMIT 2;

queries.label: Four smallest
queries.sql: SELECT amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC LIMIT 4;

lead.text: Put the times in order first, then keep the first rows.

Two orders in the shop are worth 80, so sorting on amount can't decide which of them comes first. Rows that tie can appear in either order, and the database may pick a different one the next time. A limit that cuts through a tie could keep one 80 today and the other tomorrow.

The fix is a second sort column. ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC sorts on amount first and uses id only to settle ties. Every id is different, so no tie survives it. The id is the primary key from the first lesson, which is why it makes such a dependable tie-breaker.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the tie-breaker at work on the two orders worth 20. Both results hold the same rows, and those two orders swap places. Each result is now fully decided, because the tie-breaker comes last and only matters where the earlier columns tie.

queries.label: Lower id first
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC, id ASC;

queries.label: Higher id first
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC, id DESC;

lead.text: Compare amounts first. When two rows tie, the next sort column decides.

queries.label: Lower id wins ties
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Higher id wins ties
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id DESC;

lead.text: Sorting puts the largest first, and the limit keeps the first rows of that order.
A query can filter, sort and cut at once. The filter always runs first. WHERE chooses the rows that are eligible. ORDER BY then sorts only those rows, and LIMIT keeps the first few of what is left.

So WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY amount ASC LIMIT 2 means the two smallest of the paid orders. A pending order is never considered, even a very small one. Reading the query the other way round, as the two smallest orders overall with the paid ones picked out afterwards, would let pending orders use up the places. The picture applies the same pattern to two other questions.

afterFigure.text: Each query in the picture returns one row, chosen from the rows that passed its WHERE. Read a query from the filter to the order to the limit, and its meaning follows.

queries.label: Smallest pending
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending' AND amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC, id ASC LIMIT 1;

queries.label: Largest desk
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE item = 'Desk' ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC LIMIT 1;

lead.text: WHERE chooses the eligible rows first. Then the order and the limit pick from them.

lessons.orientation: Use a deterministic order to decide which rows a limited result retains.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Five runners run a race, and the timekeeper writes their times on a clipboard in the order the runners signed up: 31, 28, 35, 30 and 29 seconds. Medals go to the three fastest.

Nobody can read the medal winners straight off the clipboard, because sign-up order says nothing about speed. The sensible move is to rewrite the times from fastest to slowest and then draw a line under the third. The order of those two moves matters. A line drawn under the third name of the original list would hand medals to the wrong people.

A table is in the same position as the clipboard. Its rows come back in no promised order, so a question such as 'the three largest orders' only makes sense once the rows have been put in an order you chose. This lesson does the sorting and the cutting, and then deals with rows that tie.

intro.promise: By the end you'll order rows so the first one means something, and keep just the top few.

recap.keyIdea: Only ORDER BY promises an order. Add a unique tie-breaker, and LIMIT keeps the first rows of that order.

blocks.text: Back at the race, you sorted first and cut second, as the medal line needs. You kept the first 3 of the ordered times and settled a tie between two 80s by id. The top three known amounts added up to 200.

recap.nextHook: A sorted list can still repeat itself. The bakery's till log that opens the next lesson holds the same few loaves over and over, and the question there is how many different ones were sold.

lessons.title: Count distinct things

lead.text: The till log has two questions hidden in it. One asks how many sales were rung up, and the answer is the length of the list. The other asks which kinds of bread were sold, and that answer is shorter, because several entries are repeats. To get it you cross off every entry that has appeared before.

A query can do the crossing off. Writing DISTINCT straight after SELECT removes repeated rows from the result, so each different value is listed once. In the shop's orders table the status column is a good place to see it. Six orders carry only two statuses, and the picture lists the column both ways.

afterFigure.text: SELECT DISTINCT status returns paid and pending once each, no matter how many orders carry them. The second query reads the same column and removes its repeats.

queries.label: Every status
queries.sql: SELECT status FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Each status once
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT status FROM orders ORDER BY status;

lead.text: Each entry in the till log is one sale.

In the orders table the customer_id column repeats, because one customer can place several orders, as the first lesson showed. Asking for that column plainly gives one entry per order. Asking for it with DISTINCT gives one entry per customer who has ordered. The orders themselves are still in the table, so DISTINCT shapes the result and leaves what is stored alone.
DISTINCT treats NULL like any other value: if a column holds several NULLs, they collapse into one NULL in the result. The picture does this with the amount column, which holds a NULL for order 106.

afterFigure.text: The second result is shorter than the first, and one of its rows is the NULL. DISTINCT removes repeats, and it doesn't remove unknowns. Asking about unknown values is a separate question, which comes up again below.

queries.label: Every amount
queries.sql: SELECT amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Each amount once
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount;

lead.text: Several orders point at the same customer.

queries.label: Every reference
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, id;

queries.label: Distinct customers
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id;

lead.text: Now the SELECT list gets a second column. DISTINCT compares the listed columns together, and two result rows count as repeats only if they match in every one of them. A row with Desk and 80 is a repeat of another row with Desk and 80, but it is a different row from one with Desk and 20.

Take the status and amount columns of the orders. Several orders are paid for 80 or for 20, so the pairs collapse. Order 106 is pending with an unknown amount, and the pair is still a row of its own. The picture shows the plain pairs and then the distinct ones.

afterFigure.text: The more columns you list, the more rows can count as different. A single column can repeat all day, and adding a column that is different in every row, such as the id, makes every row unique. DISTINCT then removes nothing at all. So choose the columns by the question you are asking.

queries.label: Every pair
queries.sql: SELECT status, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Each pair once
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT status, amount FROM orders ORDER BY status, amount;

lead.text: The orders table gives every order an id that no other order shares.
DISTINCT works on the whole selected row. This time the row is a customer paired with a status.

queries.label: Item and status
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT item, status FROM orders ORDER BY item, status;

queries.label: Customer and status
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, status FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, status;

lead.text: Often you want how many different values there are, and not the list. COUNT does the counting, and COUNT(DISTINCT day) counts the different days on which orders were placed. In the picture it sits next to the same question asked for the status column.

Counting has its own rule about unknowns. COUNT(DISTINCT x) skips NULL, because an unknown value isn't one more kind of value. SELECT DISTINCT x keeps NULL as a row of its own, as the amount column showed a moment ago. So listing the distinct values of a column and counting them can differ by one when the column holds an unknown.

afterFigure.text: Listing the different values and counting them are two questions, and a query can ask either. Pick the one that matches what you want to know. A later lesson takes counting further, and starts with the problem of what to count when some values are unknown.

queries.label: Different days
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT day) AS different_days FROM orders;

queries.label: Different statuses
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT status) AS different_statuses FROM orders;

lead.text: The amount column holds 80, 20, 80, 40, 20 and NULL.

queries.label: Distinct amounts
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount;

queries.label: Count known distinct amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

lessons.orientation: Distinguish result rows, distinct values and distinct combinations of values.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A bakery's till log for the day reads: bun, loaf, bun, roll, bun, bagel, loaf. Each entry is one sale, and the owner wants to know what the shop sold.

That is really two questions. One asks how many sales were rung up, and the answer is the length of the log. The other asks which kinds of bread sold at all, and its answer is shorter, because a bun appears three times and a loaf twice. To get it you go down the log and cross off every entry that has already appeared.

A query is in the same position. Sorting rows leaves them in a tidy order, and a sorted list can still repeat itself. This lesson shows how to ask for each different value once and how to count the different values. It also settles what 'different' means when a result has more than one column.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count different values and different combinations, and know what DISTINCT leaves alone.

recap.keyIdea: DISTINCT collapses result rows that match in every selected column. It changes the result only, so choose the columns you want to compare.

blocks.text: Back at the till log, seven sales became a shorter list of kinds. You counted 4 kinds of bread, then 3 customer ids and 5 customer and status pairs, and adding a column made more rows count as different.

recap.nextHook: Counting different values is one way to boil many rows down to one number. The next lesson turns to totals and averages, and begins with four pupils, one of whom didn't answer a survey, which raises the question of what to divide by.

lessons.title: Choose the right denominator

lead.text: Put the survey in a table, with one row for each pupil and a column for the number of books. The fourth pupil's cell is empty, which in SQL is NULL: a value nobody knows. A function that reads many rows and returns a single value is called an aggregate, and COUNT is the simplest one to start with.

COUNT comes in two forms that give different answers. COUNT(*) counts rows, so it counts every pupil whether or not the box was filled in. COUNT(books) counts the values in one column and skips the NULLs, so it counts only the pupils who gave an answer. The picture runs both on the survey.

afterFigure.text: The first query finds four pupils and the second finds three answers. The gap between the two numbers is how a missing value shows up. Every aggregate that reads a column behaves in this way: it looks at the known values and passes over the NULLs, as if those rows were absent for that column. The next screens ask what that means for totals, averages and the smallest and largest value.

queries.label: Count every pupil
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS pupils FROM survey;

queries.label: Count the answers
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(books) AS answers FROM survey;

lead.text: The shop's orders table has six rows, and the amount of order 106 is unknown. Compare counting the rows with counting the amount column.

reveal.text: You left out the unknown amount, so the column count came out one short of the row count. That gap is how a missing value shows.

queries.label: Count every order
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders;

queries.label: Count known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

lead.text: SUM and AVG pass over the empty box just as COUNT(books) did. SUM adds the values that are known. AVG adds the same values and then divides by how many there were, so the number it divides by is the count of known values and not the count of rows.

The shop's orders show it in a small case. Customer 3 has orders 105 and 106, and the amount of order 106 is unknown. Their SUM(amount) is 20, because there is only one known amount to add. Their AVG(amount) is also 20, because that one amount is divided by one and not by two. The second query in the picture counts the rows and the known amounts, so the number being divided by is on show.

afterFigure.text: An average of the known values describes the orders whose amounts we know. It says nothing about the order with the empty amount, and it is not what you would get by dividing by every order. Both numbers are honest answers to different questions, and a later screen shows how to ask for the second one. For now, remember that AVG divides by COUNT(column) and never by COUNT(*).

queries.label: Sum and average
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

queries.label: Rows and known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

lead.text: Work this one out by hand, the way AVG would.

MIN and MAX pick the smallest and the largest value in a column, and they pass over NULL like the others. An empty cell cannot be the smallest value because it holds no value at all. Reading it as a zero and expecting MIN to find it would be a mistake.

A WHERE clause runs before the aggregate and decides which rows it gets to see. Ask for MIN(amount) with a WHERE test and the function looks only at the rows that passed, and the same goes for MAX. So the order of work is to filter the rows first and then pick from what is left.

afterFigure.text: The picture runs MIN and MAX on all six orders and then on customer 3's two orders. One of those two orders has no amount, and both functions report 20, the only amount there is. The unknown order was not chosen as the smallest, and it did not drag the minimum down to zero.

queries.label: All orders
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS smallest, MAX(amount) AS largest FROM orders;

queries.label: Customer 3 only
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS smallest, MAX(amount) AS largest FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

lead.text: Pending orders are the ones whose status says pending. Filter first, then let MIN pick from the amounts that are left.

reveal.text: You picked from the known amounts of the filtered rows. An unknown amount never stands in for a smallest value.

queries.label: All orders
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS minimum, MAX(amount) AS maximum FROM orders;

queries.label: Pending only
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS minimum, MAX(amount) AS maximum FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';

lead.text: Leaving unknown values out is what an aggregate does unless it is told otherwise, and sometimes that is the wrong reading. If an empty box in the books column really means the pupil read nothing, the average ought to count that pupil.

COALESCE does the telling. COALESCE(books, 0) returns books when it is known and 0 when it is NULL, so wrapping a column in it fills every gap with 0 before the aggregate looks. AVG(COALESCE(books, 0)) then adds 4, 6, 8 and 0, and divides by 4, because the zero is now a value that counts.

afterFigure.text: On the survey that gives 4.5 and not 6. The data has not changed, only the question. 6 is the average among the pupils who answered, and 4.5 is the average if the pupil who didn't answer is taken to have read nothing. Neither is wrong, so decide which one you mean before you write the query.

queries.label: Known answers only
queries.sql: SELECT AVG(books) AS mean FROM survey;

queries.label: Blank counted as zero
queries.sql: SELECT AVG(COALESCE(books, 0)) AS mean FROM survey;

lead.text: Back to the shop's six orders, with one amount unknown. The query asks for the plain average, with nothing filled in.

reveal.text: You divided by the known amounts only. The unknown amount neither adds to the total nor counts as an order.

queries.label: Keep missing separate
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders;

queries.label: Fill missing with zero
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS total, AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS mean FROM orders;

lead.text: One case remains. A WHERE clause can remove every row, and a query that uses an aggregate still returns exactly one row, because the question still has to be answered. COUNT(*) has an easy answer: it found no rows, so it says 0.

The others have a harder time. AVG has nothing to add up and nothing to divide by, and MAX has no value to pick, so each of them reports NULL, meaning there is no result to give. COUNT is the odd one out because a count of nothing is a real number.

afterFigure.text: The picture asks for the count, the average and the largest amount among orders over 100, and there are no such orders. The answer comes back as one row holding 0, NULL and NULL. This matters when a report is built from filtered rows, because a NULL in the result can mean that nothing matched and not that the data is damaged.

queries.label: All six orders
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, AVG(amount) AS mean, MAX(amount) AS largest FROM orders;

queries.label: Amounts over 100
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, AVG(amount) AS mean, MAX(amount) AS largest FROM orders WHERE amount > 100;

lead.text: The last screen left SUM out. When WHERE leaves no rows at all, decide what the total of those rows should be.

queries.label: Known orders
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders;

queries.label: No matches
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders WHERE amount > 100;

lessons.orientation: Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX while keeping missing values visible.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Four pupils were asked how many books they read this month. Three of them answered: 4, 6 and 8. The fourth handed the form back with the box empty.

The teacher wants one number for the whole class, an average, so there is a decision to make about the empty box. Treating it as a zero says that pupil read nothing, which nobody knows. Leaving the pupil out says the class has three pupils in it, which isn't true either. The two choices give different averages, and the choice matters whether you work the figure out by hand or ask a database to do it.

A query that boils many rows down to one figure meets the same empty box every time it reaches a value nobody recorded. This lesson follows that one empty box through counting, adding, averaging and picking the smallest, to see what the database does with it and how to change that when you want to.

intro.promise: By the end you'll know which rows each summary counts, and what an unknown value does to a total or an average.

recap.keyIdea: An aggregate reads only the known values, so COUNT(column), SUM and AVG leave unknowns out of both the sum and the count, and COALESCE fills the gaps first when you want them counted.

blocks.text: You worked out an average of 6 from three answers and 48 from the shop's five known amounts. The 6 fell to 4.5 once the empty box counted as a zero. With no rows left to add, SUM came back NULL.

recap.nextHook: One average for a whole table is only the start. A café owner with a pile of slips wants a figure for each drink, and that means summarising each pile on its own.

lessons.title: Build a grouped report

lead.text: The shop's orders have the same shape as the café's slips. Each order has an amount and a status of either paid or pending. To find what each status is worth, you would deal the orders into a paid pile and a pending pile and add up each pile.

GROUP BY does the dealing. Writing GROUP BY status after the table name gathers the rows that share a status into one group, and the query then produces a single result row for each group. An aggregate such as SUM(amount) works inside each group separately, so the paid row adds the paid amounts and the pending row adds the pending ones.

afterFigure.text: Six orders go in and two rows come out. Each row of the result now stands for a status and not for an order, which is the change this whole lesson is about. The first query counts the orders in each group and the second adds their amounts. Paid is worth 200 and pending is worth 40.

queries.label: Orders in each status
queries.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

queries.label: Total of each status
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

lead.text: The café's slips are tea £2, coffee £3, tea £4, coffee £1 and tea £1. Deal them into piles by hand, the way GROUP BY would.

The grouping column decides how many rows the report has. The query gives one result row for each different value in that column, whatever the number of orders that carry it. Group the orders by day and the report has a row for every day on which something was ordered.

What can appear in the SELECT list follows from that. A result row stands for a whole group, so it can show the value the group shares, such as the day, and it can show a summary of the group, such as a count or a total. It cannot sensibly show one order's amount, because the group holds several orders.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the orders fall on four different days, so each query returns four rows. The first counts the orders on each day. The second adds their amounts, and the last day's total is NULL: its only order has no known amount, so SUM has nothing to add. A group follows the same rules for unknown values as the whole table did.

queries.label: Orders on each day
queries.sql: SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY day ORDER BY day;

queries.label: Total for each day
queries.sql: SELECT day, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY day ORDER BY day;

lead.text: Several orders share an item. Group the orders by item and think about what each result row now stands for.

reveal.text: You counted the different items. The report now has one row per item instead of one per order.

queries.label: Group by item
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Group by status
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

lead.text: Each group behaves like a small table of its own, so everything from the last lesson holds inside it. COUNT(*) counts the rows in the group. COUNT(amount) counts the group's known amounts and skips the NULLs. A total or an average covers only the known amounts of that group.

A report can show both counts side by side, and the difference between them is a warning. If a group's two counts agree, every order in it has an amount. If they differ, some amount is missing and the group's total is worth less than it looks. The picture does this for the two statuses.

afterFigure.text: Pending has two orders and one known amount, so its total of 40 comes from only half of the group. Paid has four orders and four known amounts, so nothing is missing from its 200. Showing both counts costs one extra column, and it tells the reader how far to trust each total.

queries.label: Counts in each status
queries.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

queries.label: Counts and totals
queries.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

lead.text: Inside a group, COUNT(amount) counts only that group's known amounts. The orders for each item form their own group.

reveal.text: You counted inside one group. A grouped report can show both counts, so incomplete groups stand out.

queries.label: Order counts
queries.sql: SELECT item, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Known amount counts
queries.sql: SELECT item, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

lead.text: A report often needs only some of the rows. WHERE still does that job, and in a grouped query it runs first. The database keeps the rows that pass the test, deals those rows into groups and only then adds them up. A row that fails the test never reaches a group, so it contributes nothing to any total.
The picture groups the orders by customer. The first query totals every order. The second adds WHERE status = 'paid' before the grouping, so each customer's total now covers paid orders only.

afterFigure.text: Ben's total falls from 120 to 80, because his pending lamp order, worth 40, was removed before his group was added up. Ada's orders are all paid, and Cy's one known amount is on a paid order, so neither of them changes. The test acted on single orders, which is all WHERE can see at that stage.

queries.label: Every order
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

queries.label: Paid orders only
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

lead.text: Sometimes the test is about the group and not about any single order, such as keeping only the customers whose total reaches 100. A group's total does not exist while WHERE is working, because the groups have not been made yet. WHERE cannot see it.

HAVING is the clause that can. It comes after GROUP BY and tests each group once its totals have been added up. A group that fails the test is dropped from the report, and a group that passes keeps its row. So WHERE chooses which orders go into the groups, and HAVING chooses which groups stay in the report.

afterFigure.text: The picture keeps the customers whose total is at least 100. The first query tests the totals of every order. The second also uses WHERE to keep paid orders first, so Ben's total is only 80 when HAVING looks at it, and he drops out. Reading a grouped query means reading the two tests separately, the first on rows and the second on groups.

queries.label: Totals of at least 100
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100 ORDER BY customer_id;

queries.label: Paid totals of at least 100
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100 ORDER BY customer_id;

lead.text: A report lists each item with its total, and you want to keep only the items whose total reaches a limit.

reveal.text: You named the clause that tests finished groups. Keep the row filter and the group filter apart in your head.

queries.label: Total at least 100
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100 ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Total at least 200
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 200 ORDER BY item;

lead.text: Filter the rows first, then group what is left. Read the row filter and the group filter separately.

queries.label: Every status
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Paid total at least 50
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 50 ORDER BY item;

lessons.orientation: Build a report whose rows represent groups, then filter its calculated totals.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A café keeps a slip of paper for every cup it sells. Today's pile reads: tea £2, coffee £3, tea £4, coffee £1 and tea £1. At closing time the owner doesn't want a list of cups. She wants to know how much each drink took.

You would do it without thinking. You'd deal the slips into one pile for tea and another for coffee, then add up each pile. Nobody adds the whole stack in one go, and nobody reads the slips out one at a time either. The thing the answer is about has changed from a cup to a drink.

A query can do the same dealing and adding. This lesson builds a report with one row for each pile. It then shows how to drop slips before they are dealt out, and how to drop whole piles once their totals are known.

intro.promise: By the end you'll build a report with one row for each group, and filter rows before grouping or whole groups afterwards.

recap.keyIdea: GROUP BY deals the rows into piles and gives one result row for each pile. WHERE filters rows before they are dealt, and HAVING filters the piles after their totals exist.

blocks.text: You worked out £7 of tea by dealing five slips into piles, and found 3 item groups in the orders. Inside the Lamp group only 1 amount was known, and once WHERE kept the paid orders the Desk total came to 160.

recap.nextHook: Every report so far has come from one table. The orders table holds only a customer number, though, so a report with names needs a second table. A school faces the same thing when its list of pupils holds a club number and a separate list holds the clubs.

lessons.title: Follow a relationship between tables

steps.headline: Looking up a number in another table

lead.text: A table stores each fact once. The shop's orders table records who placed an order with a customer_id, a number that is also the id of one row in the customers table. The customer's name lives only in the customers table, in the way a club's name lived only in the clubs list.

A join follows those numbers for you. JOIN customers ON customers.id = orders.customer_id pairs each order with the customer whose id equals the order's customer_id, and each pair becomes a single row holding columns from both tables. The ON condition says which values must be equal for two rows to belong together. A join that keeps only the pairs that satisfy the condition is an INNER JOIN, and a bare JOIN means the same thing.

The pupils and clubs show the same move on a small scale. If a pupil's club number is 2 and club 2 is the Choir, the pupil and the club become one row. The query makes that pairing for every pupil in a single step.
Do by hand what a join does: follow each pupil's club number to the club it names.

A join produces one result row for every pair of rows that satisfy the ON condition, and that fact explains how many rows come back. Take the pupils and the clubs. Each pupil has one club number and pairs with exactly one club, so four pupils make four pairs.

The clubs show the same thing from the other side. Chess has two pupils, so Chess appears in two rows. Choir and Drama have one pupil each. Art has none, and a club with no pupil never satisfies the condition, so it appears in no row at all. An inner join drops a row that has no partner.

afterFigure.text: Both queries in the picture return four rows, but the second starts from the clubs. A name repeats when its row has several partners, so Chess is listed twice. A name vanishes when its row has none, as Art does. Neither is a fault in the join. The result has one row for each matching pair, and its size follows the data.

queries.label: Pupils with their club
queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS pupil, c.name AS club FROM pupils AS p JOIN clubs AS c ON c.id = p.club ORDER BY p.id;

queries.label: Clubs with their pupils
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

lead.text: Orders refer to customers by number. Join the two tables on that number and think about how many matching pairs there are.

reveal.text: You counted matching pairs, not names. Each order matched the one customer it refers to, so the rows still stand for orders.

queries.label: Order references
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Names attached
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, c.name, o.amount FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

lead.text: A join gives one row for each order, so a question about customers needs one more step. To list the customers who have placed an order you join the tables and ask for the name, and each customer then appears once for every order. Writing SELECT DISTINCT before the name removes the repeats, as in the earlier lesson on different values.

afterFigure.text: The first query lists a name beside every order, six rows in all. The second keeps each name once and returns Ada, Ben and Cy. The customers table has four rows, and the result names only three of them. One customer is missing from the list, and the join is the reason.

queries.label: One row per match
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Customers who ordered
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.name;

lead.text: One customer from the table, Dee, is missing from that list. Decide what the join did with that customer's row.

A join starts from the same raw material every time: every row of one table set beside every row of the other. The ON condition then throws away the pairs that don't belong together. If you leave the condition out, nothing is thrown away. CROSS JOIN is the form with no condition, and it returns every possible pair.

Take a lunch menu with two mains and three drinks. Pairing each main with each drink gives a row for every combination, 2 × 3 = 6. The count comes from multiplying the sizes of the two tables and not from adding them. A cross join is useful when you really do want every combination, as with a menu. It is also an easy way to produce a huge result by accident, because the row count grows with the product.

afterFigure.text: The picture lists the combinations and counts them. No value in one table has to relate to a value in the other. The pairs are there simply because the condition that would have removed them is missing.

queries.label: Every combination
queries.sql: SELECT m.item AS main, d.drink FROM mains AS m CROSS JOIN drinks AS d ORDER BY m.item, d.drink;

queries.label: Count the combinations
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS combinations FROM mains CROSS JOIN drinks;

lead.text: A cross join of the shop's customers and orders has no condition, so it pairs every customer with every order.

reveal.text: You paired each customer with each order. That is not the same as the orders each customer placed.

queries.label: Match the reference
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Every possible pair
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c CROSS JOIN orders AS o ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

steps.headline: A condition that follows the number

lead.text: The ON condition is where a join can go wrong without anyone noticing. SQL accepts any condition that compares two values, whether or not the values mean the same thing. A condition that follows the stored reference pairs the right rows. A condition that compares two columns which happen to hold similar numbers pairs the wrong ones, and the query still runs.

In the school lists, a pupil's club column holds the number of a club, so p.club = c.id follows the reference. Each pupil also has an id of their own, and p.id = c.id compares a pupil's id with a club's id. Both columns hold small numbers, so the second query does return rows. Some of them are wrong.

afterFigure.text: The first query gives the true pairs. The second pairs Cy with Drama and Di with Art, because their ids happen to equal those clubs' numbers, and neither pupil is really in that club. Ann and Bo come out right by luck. A join condition should compare the column that stores the reference with the key it refers to.

queries.label: Follow the club number
queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS pupil, c.name AS club FROM pupils AS p JOIN clubs AS c ON c.id = p.club ORDER BY p.id;

queries.label: Compare the ids
queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS pupil, c.name AS club FROM pupils AS p JOIN clubs AS c ON c.id = p.id ORDER BY p.id;

lead.text: In the shop, each order stores the number of its customer and each customer has an id of their own. Pick the condition that follows that reference.

lessons.orientation: Join keys deliberately and account for every matching pair.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A school keeps two lists. The first has the pupils, and beside each name is a club number: Ann 1, Bo 2, Cy 1 and Di 3. The second has the clubs and says which number belongs to which club. Club 1, for example, is Chess.

Suppose someone asks who is in the chess club. You find Chess in the clubs list and read its number. Then you go down the pupil list looking for that number. Neither list had to carry the other's information. A number in one list pointed at a line in the other, and following the number was enough.

Databases keep their tables apart in exactly this way, so a question about customers and their orders means following numbers from one table to another. This lesson shows how a query follows the numbers for every row at once, how to tell how many rows will come back, and what happens to a row whose number points at nothing.

intro.promise: By the end you'll join two tables on their key and say how many rows to expect.

recap.keyIdea: A join pairs each row with the rows of another table whose key matches. A row with several matches repeats, and a row with none disappears from an INNER JOIN.

blocks.text: You found 2 pupils in Chess by following a club number, then counted 6 matching pairs between the shop's customers and orders. A cross join of the same tables gave 4 × 6 = 24 pairs.

recap.nextHook: An INNER JOIN drops Dee because she has no orders, and sometimes a report has to show her anyway. A librarian faces the same thing with a borrowing list: a pupil who has borrowed nothing still belongs on the list.

lessons.title: Keep the customers with no orders

steps.headline: Keeping the pupil with no books

lead.text: An INNER JOIN works like a librarian who writes down only the lines that have a book. A row with no partner leaves no trace in the result. When a report has to list everything on one side, that is the wrong tool.

LEFT JOIN is the right one. Take customers LEFT JOIN orders. The table written first is the left table, and every one of its rows appears in the result. A customer with matching orders gets a row for each order, as before. A customer with no matching order still gets one row, and the columns that should have come from orders are filled with NULL.

That NULL has a definite meaning. It says that no order matched, so there was nothing to copy into those columns. The next screens look at how such a blank behaves when you count it, test it and filter around it.
Write the list the way the librarian would, with a line for every pupil.

steps.headline: A blank that means no match

lead.text: Now the clubs are the left table, and the pupils are the rows that may or may not be there. Art has no pupils, so no pupil satisfies the ON condition for it. An INNER JOIN would drop Art. A LEFT JOIN keeps it and fills the pupil columns with NULL.

Look at the two blanks in the second result. Di's year is NULL because the school never recorded it, and Di is a real pupil. Art's pupil and year are both NULL because no pupil matched. The same symbol sits in both places and means different things. To tell them apart, look at a column that every real pupil has, such as the pupil's id.

afterFigure.text: The first query returns four rows and the second returns five. The extra row is the club with nobody in it. Everything the inner join returned is still there, so a LEFT JOIN never loses rows from the left table and never loses a match.

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil, p.year FROM clubs AS c JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

queries.label: Keep every club
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil, p.year FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

lead.text: Six orders match their customers, and one customer, Dee, has no order. Join the tables so that every customer stays.

reveal.text: You kept every match and added the customer with none. The unmatched row is still a row of the result.

queries.label: Only matches
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Keep every customer
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

lead.text: A kept row counts as a row. COUNT(*) counts every row of the result, so a club with no pupils still adds 1 to it. Often that is not the number you want. To count matches, count a column from the other table, because COUNT(column) skips the NULLs.

Not every column of the other table is safe for this. A real pupil can have an unknown year, so COUNT(p.year) would miss Di. The key column is different. Every real pupil has an id, so COUNT(p.id) is filled on every matched row and empty only on the kept one. It counts the matches exactly.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the clubs are grouped, and the first query counts rows while the second counts pupil ids. Art has one row but no pupils, so it shows 1 in the first query and 0 in the second. The other clubs agree in both queries because every row of theirs is a real match.

queries.label: Count the rows
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, COUNT(*) AS joined_rows FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Count the pupil ids
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, COUNT(p.id) AS pupils FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

lead.text: COUNT of a column ignores NULL. After the join, a customer with no match has NULL in every order column.

reveal.text: You counted matched orders, not rows. Counting a column from the right table gives zero for a customer with none.

queries.label: Count joined rows
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS rows FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Count matched orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

lead.text: A test on the other table raises a new question, because it can go in two places. Written in ON, it becomes part of the matching rule and decides which rows pair up, and a row that finds no partner is still kept with NULLs. Written in WHERE, it runs afterwards on the finished rows and removes any row that fails.

A row kept for lack of a partner has NULL in the pupil columns, and a test such as p.year = 6 is never true of NULL. In WHERE that row fails the test and disappears, so the LEFT JOIN quietly turns back into an inner join. Put the test in ON when every row of the left table has to stay.

afterFigure.text: The picture asks for the clubs with their year 6 pupils. With the test in ON, all four clubs are still listed. Chess and Choir show a year 6 pupil, and Drama and Art show NULL because nobody in year 6 matched them. With the test in WHERE, only the two clubs that have a year 6 pupil remain.

queries.label: Test in ON
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id AND p.year = 6 ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

queries.label: Test in WHERE
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id WHERE p.year = 6 ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

lead.text: In Dee's row every orders column is NULL. A test written after the join runs on those NULLs.

reveal.text: You decided where the paid test belongs. A test in ON limits which orders match. A test in WHERE can remove the preserved customer.

queries.label: Version one
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Version two
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

lead.text: A kept row can be picked out with IS NULL, which you met earlier for unknown values. The question is which column to test. A column that the other table can leave unknown on a real row gives a muddled answer, because the test then finds both kinds of blank.

The pupils show it. Di is a real pupil whose year was never recorded, so p.year IS NULL is true for Di and for the kept row of Art. The key column p.id is filled on every real pupil, so p.id IS NULL is true only where nothing matched. Testing the key finds exactly the clubs with no pupils.

afterFigure.text: The first query tests the key and returns Art alone. The second tests the year and returns Drama and Art, which are different kinds of row. When you want the rows with no match, test a column that a matched row always has.

queries.label: Test the key
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id WHERE p.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Test the year
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id WHERE p.year IS NULL ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

lead.text: The shop's customers are the left table and the orders are the other. Pick the test that finds only the customers with no order.

lessons.orientation: Preserve unmatched customers without counting them as orders.
lessons.reviewLabel: Keep the customers with no orders
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A librarian lists each pupil beside the books they have borrowed. Ann borrowed 2, Bo borrowed 1 and Cy borrowed none. The head teacher wants a list of every pupil with the books they have out, so she can see at a glance who has been using the library.

If the librarian writes only the lines that have a book, Cy never appears, and the list suggests that the school has two pupils. To show everyone she writes a line for Cy as well and leaves the book blank. The blank has a definite meaning: no book matched Cy.

The last lesson's join drops a row that has no partner. This lesson keeps it, and shows how to count and test the blanks that result, so that a missing partner is never mistaken for a missing value inside a row that did have one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll keep customers who have no orders, and tell a missing match from a missing amount.

recap.keyIdea: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and fills the other table's columns with NULL where nothing matched. Count and test the other table's key to tell a missing match from a missing value.

blocks.text: You wrote 4 lines for 3 pupils and counted 7 rows once Dee was kept. Her COUNT(o.id) was 0, because no order matched.

recap.nextHook: A LEFT JOIN protects only the table written first. Sometimes both lists have people missing from the other: guests who replied but have no badge, and badges printed for people who never replied. Keeping everyone from both sides is the next step.

lessons.title: Keep unmatched rows on either side

steps.headline: Left, right and the mirror image

lead.text: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the table written first. When the unmatched rows that matter are in the other table, you want the mirror image. That is RIGHT JOIN, which keeps every row of the table written second and puts NULL on the left wherever a row there has no partner.

The party lists show both. Ana replied but has no badge, so she has no partner in the badge list. Dot has a badge but never replied, so she has none in the reply list. Ben and Cy are on both lists. A LEFT JOIN from the replies to the badges keeps Ana. A RIGHT JOIN keeps Dot. Which one to use depends on whose missing partner you care about.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the first query starts from the replies and keeps all three guests, with Ana's badge blank. The second keeps all three badges, with Dot's reply blank. Each has three rows, and each drops one of the two unmatched people. Neither is wrong, because each answers a different question.

queries.label: Keep every reply
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g LEFT JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY g.name;

queries.label: Keep every badge
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g RIGHT JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY b.name;

lead.text: Make the combined list by hand, with a line for everyone who is on either list.

Sometimes neither side may lose anyone. The combined guest list needs Ana from one list and Dot from the other, along with the people on both. FULL OUTER JOIN does that. It returns every matched pair, then adds each unmatched row of the left table with NULLs on the right, and each unmatched row of the right table with NULLs on the left.

That gives a way to count the result. The number of rows is the number of matched pairs, plus the unmatched rows on the left, plus the unmatched rows on the right. An unmatched left row is never paired with an unmatched right row, because their keys differ, so each stays in a row of its own.

afterFigure.text: The first query in the picture is an inner join and returns two rows, for Ben and Cy. The second is the full join. It returns four: the two matches, Ana with a blank badge and Dot with a blank reply. Reading the NULLs shows who is missing from which list.

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g INNER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY g.name;

queries.label: Keep both sides
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY COALESCE(g.name, b.name);

lead.text: The shop's orders now include a guest order, 107, with no customer. Dee still has no order. Each join preserves one side.

reveal.text: You picked the side that RIGHT keeps: the table written on the right. Its unmatched row stays, and the other side's unmatched row is dropped.

queries.label: Preserve customers
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Preserve orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c RIGHT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

lead.text: The same two tables, with guest order 107 included. A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps the matched pairs and the unmatched rows from both sides.

reveal.text: You added the matches to the unmatched rows from each side. Both kinds of absence are rows of the result.

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c INNER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Preserve both sides
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

lead.text: With the guest order in the table, the shop has a customer with no order and an order with no customer. A LEFT JOIN from customers to orders keeps Dee and loses the guest order. A RIGHT JOIN keeps the guest order and loses Dee. Each returns seven rows: six matched pairs plus one kept row.

Equal counts do not mean equal results. Two joins can return the same number of rows while keeping different records, and only the NULLs show which side was kept. Look for the blanks in a result before you trust its size.

afterFigure.text: One more fact helps with counting. A RIGHT JOIN returns at least one row for every row of the right table, and exactly one when each of those rows matches no more than one row on the left. A right table of five rows that each match at most once gives five rows, wherever the matches fall.

queries.label: Preserve customers
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Preserve orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c RIGHT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

lead.text: After a full join the NULLs say which side lacked a partner. If the guest column is NULL, the row is a badge with no reply. If the badge column is NULL, the row is a reply with no badge. Testing one side's key with IS NULL picks out the rows where that side was missing.
As in the last lesson, choose a key that is always filled on a real row, such as the name. A real row cannot have a NULL there, so a NULL always means that nothing matched.

afterFigure.text: The first query asks for the rows where the badge is NULL and finds Ana, who replied and has no badge. The second asks for the rows where the guest is NULL and finds Dot. A count of rows cannot tell the two apart, but the blanks can.

queries.label: Badge is NULL
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name WHERE b.name IS NULL ORDER BY g.name;

queries.label: Guest is NULL
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name WHERE g.name IS NULL ORDER BY b.name;

lead.text: The shop's customers and orders are joined again, with every unmatched row kept. Think about which side a NULL key points to.

reveal.text: You read the NULL key to see which side was absent. A row count alone cannot tell you that.

queries.label: First test
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Second test
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

steps.headline: A test in the ON condition

lead.text: A condition in ON decides which rows can pair. In a full join a row that fails the condition is kept as an unmatched row on its own side, and so adding a test to ON can create more unmatched rows.
