Suppose the badges have colours, and the rule is to pair a guest only with a blue badge. Ben's badge is blue, so Ben still pairs. Cy's badge is red, so the pair fails the rule. Cy the guest and Cy the badge are now two unmatched rows, one on each side.

afterFigure.text: The first query matches on name alone and returns four rows. The second adds the colour test and returns five: Ben's pair, then Ana and Cy as replies with no badge, then Cy and Dot as badges with no reply. The test removed nothing. It turned one matched row for Cy into two unmatched ones.

queries.label: Match on name
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY COALESCE(g.name, b.name);

queries.label: Match on name and blue
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name AND b.colour = 'blue' ORDER BY COALESCE(g.name, b.name), b.name;

lead.text: The paid test now sits in the ON condition of the full join. Orders that fail it stay in the result as unmatched rows.

queries.label: Match every status
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Only paid matches
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid' WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

lessons.orientation: Compare RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN with a guest order that has no customer reference.
lessons.reviewLabel: Keep unmatched rows on either side
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A party organiser has two lists. The reply list has the guests who said they were coming: Ana, Ben and Cy. The badge list has the names that were printed on badges: Ben, Cy and Dot. The two lists mostly agree, but not entirely.

The organiser wants one list of everyone who appears on either. Ben and Cy are on both lists and go down once each. Ana replied but has no badge, so she goes down anyway. Dot has a badge but never replied, and she goes down too. Keeping only the names that appear on both lists would lose two people who matter.

The last lesson kept the customer with no orders. This one keeps unmatched rows from either side, so that nobody is lost from a list because the other list has no partner for them. It also covers what the blanks in the combined list tell you.

intro.promise: By the end you'll choose which side of a join to preserve, and read the NULLs that show who is missing.

recap.keyIdea: A RIGHT JOIN preserves the right table and a FULL OUTER JOIN preserves both. A NULL key shows which side had no match.

blocks.text: You combined two lists into 4 names, then counted 8 rows in the full join of the shop's tables. With the paid test in the ON condition, 3 order rows had no customer.

recap.nextHook: Joins settle which rows from two tables belong together. Some questions need an answer that the table itself has to supply first, such as a class average that decides who gets a sticker. The next lesson puts one query inside another to get it.

lessons.title: Use one query to define another

lead.text: The teacher's two passes carry straight over into SQL. We'll use the shop's orders again: six orders, five with a known amount (80, 20, 80, 40 and 20) and one, order 106, whose amount isn't known yet. The question is which orders are worth more than the average order.

The first pass is a query of its own: SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders. It adds up the known amounts, 240 altogether, and divides by the five orders that have one, which gives 48. An order with an unknown amount is left out of both the sum and the count.

afterFigure.text: Now for the second pass. Write the first query in brackets and put it where the number would go: WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders). A query written inside another one like this is called a subquery. SQL runs the subquery first and gets one number back. The outer query then compares every order with that number, just as the teacher compared each score with the figure in her margin.
A subquery that returns one number is the simplest case. Sometimes the first pass has to produce a whole list instead, and after two questions on the average the lesson turns to that.

queries.label: The average on its own
queries.sql: SELECT AVG(amount) AS average FROM orders;

queries.label: What the average is built from
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

lead.text: Do it the teacher's way. Find the average first, then compare each score with it.
The shop's orders get the same treatment. The subquery works out the average amount first, and the outer query keeps the orders above it. Think about which of the five known amounts pass.

reveal.text: You compared each amount with the average the subquery found. An amount equal to it would not pass a strict comparison.

queries.label: Above the average
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Strictly above 80
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 80 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: So far the inside query has handed back one number. It can just as well hand back a column of values, and the outer query can then check whether a row's value is on that list. The test is written IN: a row passes when its value is among the values the subquery returns.

Suppose the shop wants every order placed by a customer in the North region. The orders table doesn't know where anyone lives. It stores only a customer_id, and the region sits in the customers table. So the first pass looks up the North customers with SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'North' and gets a short list of ids. The second pass keeps any order whose customer_id is on that list.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the first pass alone, for two regions. IN asks only whether a value is on the list. A long list never repeats an order, and the outer result still has one row per order. The amount plays no part in the test. Whenever a customer is on the list, all of that customer's orders are kept, including any whose amount is unknown.

queries.label: The North list
queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE region = 'North' ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The South list
queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE region = 'South' ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Find the North customers first, then count the orders that point at them.

reveal.text: You found the customers first and then their orders. An order with an unknown amount still counts: IN looks at the customer.

queries.label: North customers' orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'North') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: South customers' orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'South') ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Sometimes the outer query doesn't need the matching values at all. It only needs to know whether there are any. Take the shop's customers and ask which of them have placed at least one order. The question is put to one customer at a time.

EXISTS puts that question in brackets. For each customer, the subquery looks through the orders for one whose customer_id is that customer's id, and EXISTS says yes as soon as it finds a single row. Ada has two orders, and she is still listed once, because the question is only whether a match is there. The number of matches never changes the answer. Put NOT in front and the test flips, keeping the customers for whom the search comes back empty.

afterFigure.text: The first query in the figure keeps Ada, Ben and Cy. The second keeps Dee, who has placed nothing. Look at the inside query: it mentions c.id, the id of the customer being asked about at that moment. That means it can't be run once and then forgotten. It has to be run again for each customer, and a later screen comes back to why that matters.

queries.label: At least one order
queries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: No orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

lead.text: Ada has two orders in the table, yet the EXISTS query lists her on a single line.

steps.headline: An inside query that changes with the row

lead.text: The inside query for EXISTS used the customer being asked about, so its answer depended on which customer that was. A subquery that refers to a value from the current row of the outer query is called correlated. It can't be worked out once in advance, as the average could, so SQL works it out again for every outer row.

Some comparisons need exactly that. Instead of comparing each order with the average for everyone, compare it with the average for its own customer. Ada's orders are 80 and 20, an average of 50, so her 80 is above her own average and her 20 is below it. Ben's are 80 and 40, an average of 60. Cy has a single known amount, 20, which is its own average.

afterFigure.text: Only orders 101 and 103 pass, Ada's 80 and Ben's 80. Cy's order fails because an amount equal to the average is not above it. A strict greater-than never lets equal values through, which is worth remembering for the next question.

queries.label: Each customer's average
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, AVG(amount) AS average FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

queries.label: Above their own customer's average
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.amount FROM orders AS o WHERE o.amount > (SELECT AVG(i.amount) FROM orders AS i WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id) ORDER BY o.id;

lead.text: Now compare each order with the average for its own item, not its own customer. Desk, Book and Lamp each have an average of their known amounts.

reveal.text: You compared each amount with its own item's average. Every known amount equals that average, and equal is not above.

queries.label: Above overall average
queries.sql: SELECT id, item, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Above its item average
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, o.item, o.amount FROM orders AS o WHERE o.amount > (SELECT AVG(i.amount) FROM orders AS i WHERE i.item = o.item) ORDER BY o.id;

lessons.orientation: Use scalar subqueries, IN and EXISTS without multiplying the outer result.
lessons.reviewLabel: Use one query to define another
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A teacher has marked six tests. The scores are 10, 50, 60, 70, 80 and 90, and she has promised a sticker to everyone who scored above the class average. She can't tell who has earned one by reading down the list, because she doesn't yet know what the average is.

So she works in two passes. First she adds the scores up, divides by six and jots the answer in the margin. Only then does she go back to the top and compare each pupil's score with the number in the margin. The first pass is there to feed the second.

A database has the same difficulty. Asking for the orders above the average order needs the average before a single order can be judged. SQL lets you write the first pass inside the second. This lesson starts with the simplest case. The inside query hands back one number, and the lesson builds up from there.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write queries that take their comparison from another query placed inside them.

recap.keyIdea: A subquery supplies a value, a list or a yes-or-no test to an outer query. A correlated one is worked out again for each outer row.

blocks.text: You found 3 pupils above a class average of 60 and 2 orders above the shop's average of 48. North customers had 4 orders, and no order sat strictly above the average for its own item.

recap.nextHook: A subquery lets one question borrow the answer to another. Two questions can also share a page, as when a head teacher wants the chess club's pupils and the drama club's pupils on a single list. The next lesson stacks two results into one.

lessons.title: Combine reports deliberately

lead.text: A join lays two tables side by side, matching rows and adding columns. The head teacher's job runs the other way. Both clubs hold the same kind of information, a column of names. What is wanted is a single longer column. The tool for that is UNION, which writes the rows of one query's result beneath the rows of another's.

UNION has two requirements. Both queries must return the same number of columns, since their rows are going to line up in a single table. The columns are matched by position, first with first and second with second, whatever they are called, so each position should hold the same sort of value. The two queries may read different tables or the same one, and their results can be different lengths.

afterFigure.text: The figure holds a single table, members, with one line for each pupil and club. Each club's query on its own gives four names. UNION takes those two results and returns the rows of both. Any row that has already appeared is dropped, so every different row is kept once, and that is how the head's eight lines shrink to the pupils who are actually there.

queries.label: Chess club
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: Drama club
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

lead.text: Do by hand what UNION does with the two clubs' lists.

Dropping repeats suits a register, but not every report. A coach company booking places for each club's outing would want Cy and Di counted once for chess and once for drama. UNION ALL gives that. It stacks the two results and keeps every row, so a pupil who comes back from both queries appears twice.

The two forms differ in one more way. UNION has to compare rows to find the repeats, while UNION ALL simply writes one result under the other. The row counts follow a short rule. UNION ALL returns the size of the first result plus the size of the second. UNION returns that same total minus every row it drops as a repeat.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, UNION returns the six pupils and UNION ALL returns all eight lines, with Cy and Di twice. Both are correct. They answer different questions, so choose by what the count of rows is meant to say.

queries.label: Remove repeated rows
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: Keep every row
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION ALL SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

lead.text: Work out each query's list of ids first, then decide what UNION does with an id that both lists contain.

reveal.text: You removed the ids that both queries returned. Plain UNION counts each different row once.

queries.label: Remove repeated rows
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Keep occurrences
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION ALL SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: When two rows are the same row

lead.text: UNION decides whether a row is a repeat by comparing the whole row, every column of it. Two rows are the same only when each value matches its partner. If the club lists carried a second column naming the club, Cy from chess and Cy from drama would no longer be the same row, because the clubs differ.

That gives a way to keep context that a bare list of names loses. Add a label to each query to keep it. One query selects name together with 'chess' AS club, and the other selects name together with 'drama' AS club. The label is a fixed piece of text written into every row of its query, so rows from different queries differ in at least one column and nothing can collapse. UNION then behaves like UNION ALL, although it still checks.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the plain list of names gives six rows and the labelled list gives eight, because Cy and Di now appear once under each club. Whether you want that depends on the question. Include a column only if its value belongs in the report, since every extra column is another place for two rows to differ.

queries.label: Names only
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: Names and club
queries.sql: SELECT name, 'chess' AS club FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name, 'drama' AS club FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name, club;

lead.text: UNION compares the whole row. Put the id and the label together before you decide which rows repeat.

reveal.text: You compared the id and the label together. A label turns a repeat into a new row.

queries.label: Id only
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Id and selection label
queries.sql: SELECT id, 'paid' AS selection FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id, 'large' AS selection FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id, selection;

lead.text: A stacked result has no particular order, because UNION is free to return the rows in whichever order suits it. A report needs a fixed order, and ORDER BY supplies one. Written once, after the last query, it sorts the whole combined result.

Two things follow from that position. The sort runs after the repeats have gone, so it orders only the rows that survived. LIMIT sits in the same place and counts from the top of the sorted, combined list. Asking for the first three names from the two club lists, in alphabetical order, gives Ann, Bo and Cy, and Cy takes third place once, since the repeat was removed before the counting began.

afterFigure.text: Only the ORDER BY at the end sorts the finished list. The order of each query on its own is lost once the results are stacked, so there is no point in sorting them first.

queries.label: The combined list, sorted
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: The first three names
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name LIMIT 3;

lead.text: Back to the shop's orders. UNION removes repeats first, and ORDER BY then sorts what is left.

queries.label: Combined result
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: First three combined ids
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id LIMIT 3;

lessons.orientation: Stack compatible results with UNION or UNION ALL and account for overlapping rows.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: The chess club has four members: Ann, Bo, Cy and Di. The drama club has four as well: Cy, Di, Ed and Flo. The head teacher needs a single list of every pupil who belongs to either club, for a trip permission slip.
Copying one club's list under the other gives eight lines. Cy and Di belong to both clubs and so are written twice. The head wants every pupil written once.

Each club's list is itself the result of a query. This lesson is about writing two such results one above the other and deciding what to do with the pupils who turn up in both. Along the way it works out what counts as the same line when a list has more than one column.

intro.promise: By the end you'll stack two query results into one list, and say which repeated rows stay and which collapse.

recap.keyIdea: UNION stacks results of the same shape and removes repeated rows. UNION ALL keeps every occurrence, and a differing column keeps rows apart.

blocks.text: You counted 6 names on the head's list, then found 5 rows under UNION and 7 once the labels differed. The third id in the sorted list was 103.

recap.nextHook: UNION made one list out of two. A list can also carry positions, such as who came first and who came second. Positions get awkward when two rows are equal, as when two runners cross a finish line together. The next lesson ranks rows and settles what a tie should do.

lessons.title: Rank rows without collapsing them

lead.text: Earlier lessons collapsed rows. GROUP BY turns a table of orders into one line for each customer, and the individual orders disappear into their totals. A results board can't work like that, because every runner needs a line of their own with a position beside it. What the board needs is a calculation that adds a value to each row and leaves the rows where they are.

That is what a window function does. The window is the set of rows the calculation is allowed to look at, and the function works out its value for one row at a time. You write it as the function followed by OVER, with the order to use in brackets. The simplest is ROW_NUMBER, which hands out 1, 2, 3 down the rows in the stated order.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets the two side by side on the shop's orders. The grouped query returns three lines, one for each customer. The window query returns all six orders, each with its position. The ORDER BY inside the brackets decides which row counts as first, so the numbering is only as sensible as that order is. A different ORDER BY would number the same rows differently.

queries.label: Grouped
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

queries.label: Windowed
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The ORDER BY inside OVER decides who counts as first.

ROW_NUMBER always separates the rows. When two rows are equal it still gives one of them the smaller number, and the choice between them is arbitrary. A results board wants something different for a tie: equal rows should get equal positions.

RANK does that. Rows that tie get the same rank, and the next row's rank is one more than the number of rows ahead of it. Picture a diving contest in which Eve, Fay and Gus all score 9 and Hal scores 7. The three at the top share first place. Three divers are ahead of Hal, which makes him fourth. Nobody is second or third, and the gap is deliberate, because the rank says how many divers finished ahead.

afterFigure.text: The figure gives the same contest both ways. ROW_NUMBER splits the three top scorers into 1, 2 and 3, while RANK puts all three on 1 and then jumps to 4. Counting the rows ahead is the whole rule, so you can check any rank by counting how many rows have a better value and adding one.

queries.label: Every row numbered
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC, name) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position;

queries.label: Tied rows share a rank
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position, name;

lead.text: Use the rule from the diving contest. Count the runners who finished ahead.
Order the amounts largest first, then count the rows that come before the 40.

reveal.text: You counted the rows ahead and added one. Ties are part of that count, which is why RANK can leave gaps.

queries.label: Number each row
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Share ranks for equal amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lead.text: RANK's jump from 1 to 4 suits a results board, because a place says how many finished ahead. A table of prizes can need the opposite. If prizes go to first and second place, a diver behind the three joint leaders should still take second, with no missing positions.

DENSE_RANK does that. Tied rows share a rank, as they do under RANK, but the next rank is just one more than the previous rank, whatever the size of the tie. It counts different values ahead and adds one, where RANK counts rows ahead and adds one. Hal is second, because only one different score, 9, is higher than his 7.

afterFigure.text: The figure puts the two side by side. The top three get 1 under both. Under RANK Hal is 4th, and under DENSE_RANK he is 2nd. Neither rule is wrong, since the right choice depends on what a position should mean in the report.

queries.label: Ranks with gaps
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position, name;

queries.label: Ranks without gaps
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position, name;

lead.text: Count the different amounts above the 40, then add one.

reveal.text: You counted different amounts, not rows. Choose RANK or DENSE_RANK by what the report should mean.

queries.label: Ranks with gaps
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Ranks without gaps
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lead.text: A tie is only a tie while the window can't tell two rows apart. The window compares rows using everything inside its ORDER BY, so a second column can separate rows that the first leaves level. Eve, Fay and Gus all scored 9, but their names differ, and putting the name after the score tells the window how to put them in order.

With that second column in place the three are no longer equal. RANK now gives them 1, 2 and 3, because each has a different number of divers ahead of it, and Hal stays fourth. The result looks just like ROW_NUMBER's, which gives a useful rule of thumb. If the ORDER BY puts every row in a different place in the line, the ties are gone and ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK all agree.

afterFigure.text: The figure ranks the contest twice. The first query orders by points alone, so the three scores of 9 tie. The second adds the name, and the tie breaks into three separate places. Add a tie-breaker when a report must pick exactly one winner, and leave it out when equal values really should share a place.

queries.label: Points only
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position, name;

queries.label: Points, then name
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC, name) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position;

lead.text: The window compares rows by everything in its ORDER BY. Think about what an extra column does to two rows that are level.

queries.label: Rank the amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Rank amount and id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lessons.orientation: Distinguish ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK and choose tie behaviour deliberately.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Four runners cross the finish line in 10, 10, 12 and 14 seconds. The two fastest reach it together, so the organiser's results board has to say something about the tie. The rule is that runners with equal times share a place.

That is easy to say and awkward to write down. If two runners share first place, the next runner is third by some ways of counting and second by others, and the board has to follow a single rule for everyone. The last runner's place depends on which rule it is.

Ranking the rows of a table raises the same choice. A report that lists every row with a position beside it needs a rule for equal values, and SQL offers several. This lesson numbers the rows first and then follows the race's tie through each rule.

intro.promise: By the end you'll put a position beside every row and say how each way of numbering treats ties.

recap.keyIdea: A window function ranks rows without collapsing them. ROW_NUMBER never ties. RANK leaves gaps after ties, and DENSE_RANK does not.

blocks.text: You placed the 14-second runner 4th, then ranked the amount 40 as 3 with RANK and 2 with DENSE_RANK. Adding id to the ordering split the tie at 80.

recap.nextHook: Every ranking so far treated the table as one race. Often the rows belong to separate groups that should each be ranked or totalled on their own, like the pupils of different classes on one mark sheet. The next lesson splits a window into groups.

lessons.title: Choose which rows a window sees

lead.text: In the last lesson the window was the whole table, put in some order. A window can be narrowed so that each row sees only some of the rows. PARTITION BY names the column that decides which rows belong together, and the rows that share a value in it form a window of their own. It goes inside the brackets after OVER, ahead of any ORDER BY.

Take the shop's orders and give each customer a window. SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) adds up the amounts inside the customer's own window and writes the answer beside every one of that customer's orders. Ada's two orders, 80 and 20, both show 100. Ben's both show 120. The window only gathers rows for the calculation, so every order keeps its own line, where GROUP BY would have merged them.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the windowed totals above the grouped ones. Cy's two orders both show 20, because the unknown amount on order 106 adds nothing to the sum. The grouped version gives the same three totals, but only one line for each customer.

queries.label: Totals beside the orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Totals as groups
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS customer_total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

lead.text: Work as the window does. Find the pupil's own class, then add up that class and no other.
Now partition by status instead. The paid orders form one window and the pending orders form another.

reveal.text: You added inside one window. The total repeats beside each of its orders.

queries.label: Group the report
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

queries.label: Keep rows with status totals
queries.sql: SELECT id, status, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY status) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The numbering and ranking functions from the last lesson respect a partition too. Each window starts afresh, so a ROW_NUMBER with a partition begins at 1 in every group. Without the partition the numbers run on through the whole table.

Go back to the mark sheet and number the pupils from the highest score down. Over the whole sheet Bo (8) is numbered 1, Ann (6) is 2 and Cy (5) is 3. Partition by class and Cy's number changes, because Cy is the only pupil in class B and so comes first in that window. Ann and Bo are still numbered 2 and 1.

afterFigure.text: A number from a partitioned window says where the row stands among the rows of its own group, which is usually what a report is asking. The same holds for RANK and DENSE_RANK, and for every running calculation you meet later.

queries.label: One window for the whole sheet
queries.sql: SELECT name, class, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM pupils ORDER BY position;

queries.label: A window for each class
queries.sql: SELECT name, class, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY class ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM pupils ORDER BY class, position;

lead.text: Each customer's orders are numbered from the lowest id upwards, starting afresh for every customer.

reveal.text: You followed the numbering into one customer's window. It restarts where a new customer begins.

queries.label: One global window
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: One window per customer
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A window can also be cut into bands of equal size, such as the better and the worse half of a class. NTILE(n) does this. It lines the rows up in the stated order and deals them into n buckets, numbered from 1, so that no two buckets differ in size by more than one row. When the rows don't divide evenly, the first buckets are the larger ones.

Ten rows in four buckets show how the extras are placed. Four buckets of two use up eight rows and leave two extras. The extras go to the first two buckets, so the sizes are 3, 3, 2 and 2. Which bucket a row lands in depends on its position in the order, so rows with the same score can end up in different buckets. NTILE divides rows and takes no notice of how many different values there are.

afterFigure.text: The figure orders ten pupils by id and cuts them into four buckets, then into three. Use NTILE when a report needs groups of roughly equal size, such as the top quarter of scorers. Like the other window functions it can be partitioned, which cuts each group on its own.

queries.label: Four buckets
queries.sql: SELECT id, pupil, score, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM marks ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Three buckets
queries.sql: SELECT id, pupil, score, NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM marks ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The shop's five orders with a known amount are dealt into three buckets, larger buckets first.

reveal.text: You shared rows out by position. Buckets divide rows, not different amounts.

queries.label: Split A
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, NTILE(2) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Split B
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The last job is to keep only some rows according to a window value, such as the first order of each customer, which is the row numbered 1 in a partitioned numbering. The obvious attempt is to write position = 1 in the WHERE clause of the same query.

That doesn't work, and the reason is the order in which a query is evaluated. WHERE decides which rows are kept before any window function is worked out, so the number doesn't exist yet when WHERE goes looking for it. The numbers appear in the SELECT list, which comes later.

afterFigure.text: The fix is to number the rows in an inner query and filter on the number in an outer one, as in the second query of the figure. The outer query sees the position as an ordinary column of the inner query's result, so WHERE position = 1 now has something to test. The figure keeps Bo for class A and Cy for class B.

queries.label: Every pupil numbered
queries.sql: SELECT name, class, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY class ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM pupils ORDER BY class, position;

queries.label: The top pupil in each class
queries.sql: SELECT name, class, score FROM (SELECT name, class, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY class ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM pupils) WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY class;

lead.text: The shop wants each customer's first order, which means keeping the rows numbered 1.

queries.label: Number all customer orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: First order per customer
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, position FROM (SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders) WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Calculate within each row's group and filter the resulting values.
lessons.reviewLabel: Choose which rows a window sees
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A teacher has a mark sheet for two classes. Class A has two pupils, who scored 6 and 8. Class B has one pupil, who scored 5. She wants every pupil's line to show the total for their own class, so that a parent reading one line can see how the class as a whole did.

Two quick fixes both fail. A single total for the whole sheet would put 19 on every line, which mixes the classes together. Collapsing each class into one line gives the right totals but loses the pupils, and the sheet is meant to keep a line for each pupil. What she needs is a total worked out inside each class and written beside every line in that class.

Last lesson's rankings treated the table as one group. This lesson splits it into groups first, so that each calculation starts afresh inside its own group. The same idea then carries on to numbering, and the lesson ends by picking out one row from each group.

intro.promise: By the end you'll make a calculation restart inside each group, and filter rows on the value it produces.

recap.keyIdea: PARTITION BY gives each group its own window. Calculations restart inside it, and filtering on the result needs an outer query.

blocks.text: You wrote a class total of 14, then restarted numbering at 1 for customer 2. A paid total of 200 sat beside each paid order, and five orders split into buckets of 2, 2 and 1.

recap.nextHook: A total beside each line covers the whole group. A bank statement asks for something different: each line shows the balance so far, a total of only the lines above it. The next lesson builds those running figures and reads the rows just before and after.

lessons.title: Read the rows before and after

lead.text: Think about the statement again. Each balance is a sum, but a different set of rows is added at every line: one deposit at line one, two at line two, three at line three. The window needs a way to say which rows to add for the row it is on.

That is the frame, the stretch of the window that the calculation uses for the current row. Writing ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW sets the frame to every row from the start of the window down to the current one. SUM over that frame gives a running total, a sum that grows by one row at each step. The ORDER BY inside OVER matters here, because it decides which row is first and so which rows count as coming before.

afterFigure.text: The figure follows a money jar with four deposits: 20, 5, 15 and 10. The running total, 20, 25, 40 and 50, is the sum of the frame at each line. As with any SUM, an unknown amount adds nothing and does not stop the total growing on later lines. The jar also records the day of each deposit, and two questions from now that column starts to matter.

queries.label: The whole total on every row
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER () AS total FROM jar ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The total so far
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM jar ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Each line adds one more row to the frame. Work out the third line of the statement.
The shop's orders in id order. The frame runs from the first order to the current one, and the last amount is unknown, so it adds nothing.

reveal.text: You added the rows up to and including the current one. The grand total would use every row at once.

queries.label: Known grand total
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER () AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Running known total
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: Rows that tie in the order

lead.text: One detail of the frame needs care when two rows tie in the ordering. Look at the money jar: two deposits were made on day 2. If the window is ordered by day alone, nothing says which of the two comes first.

ROWS counts physical rows. It takes them one at a time, so the first of the two day-2 deposits gets its own running total and the second adds to it. RANGE works by value instead. Rows that tie on the ordering value are called peers, and RANGE treats them as a single step, so every peer joins the frame together. Both day-2 deposits show the same running total, which includes the pair in full.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the first query gives 20, 25, 40 and 50, and the second gives 20, 40, 40 and 50. They agree everywhere except across the tied pair. When a window has an ORDER BY and no frame is written, SQL uses the RANGE version, so a running total over a column with repeats can jump by two rows at once. Writing the ROWS frame yourself removes the surprise.

queries.label: Counting rows
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM jar ORDER BY day, id;

queries.label: Counting by day
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM jar ORDER BY day, id;

lead.text: Decide which rows the frame holds for each of the two September 2 orders.

queries.label: ROWS frame
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY day, id;

queries.label: RANGE frame
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY day, id;

lead.text: A frame adds rows up. Sometimes a report needs a single neighbour instead, such as the previous deposit, to see how the new one compares. LAG(amount) returns the amount from the row before the current one in the window's order.

The first row has nothing before it, so LAG gives NULL there. The order inside OVER decides what before means, so the same table read in the opposite order hands back different neighbours. Read the jar's deposits from newest to oldest and the row before a deposit is the one made after it.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the jar read both ways. In day order the second deposit sees 20 behind it. Read backwards, the first deposit sees 5, because 5 sits one row earlier in that reversed order. Subtract LAG's value from the current amount and you have the change since the previous line.

queries.label: Reading forwards
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ASC) AS previous FROM jar ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Reading backwards
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id DESC) AS previous FROM jar ORDER BY id DESC;

lead.text: The shop's orders, read in increasing id order. LAG looks one row back.

reveal.text: You read one row back in the stated order. Reversing the order would change which row counts as previous.

queries.label: Previous in increasing id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ASC) AS previous FROM orders ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Previous in decreasing id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id DESC) AS previous FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC;

steps.headline: Looking ahead, and what a blank means

lead.text: LEAD is the mirror of LAG. It returns the value from the next row in the window's order, and the last row has nothing after it, so LEAD gives NULL there. Between them, LAG and LEAD let a row see both of its neighbours without a join.

A NULL from either function has two possible causes. There may be no neighbour in that direction, as at the ends. Or the neighbour is there and its own value is unknown. Take a water meter read on three days: 12 litres on day 1, no reading on day 2 and 9 litres on day 3. LEAD of the litres gives NULL on day 1 and on day 3, for different reasons. Day 2's reading is missing, and nothing follows day 3.

afterFigure.text: To tell the two causes apart, read a column that is always filled in. LEAD of the day number is NULL only where no next row exists, so the figure shows it beside LEAD of the litres. A NULL in the first and a number in the second means the neighbour is there and its value is missing.

queries.label: The next reading
queries.sql: SELECT id, litres, LEAD(litres) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_litres FROM meter ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The next day
queries.sql: SELECT id, litres, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id FROM meter ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Back in the shop's orders, in increasing id order. LEAD looks one row ahead.

queries.label: Next amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Next id
queries.sql: SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Specify running frames and use LAG or LEAD with an explicit ordering.
lessons.reviewLabel: Read the rows before and after
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A bank statement lists three deposits in the order they were made: 30 pounds, then 10, then 50. Beside each deposit the bank prints the balance, the amount in the account as of that line.

The balance on the first line is 30, since nothing came before it. On the second line it covers the first deposit and the second. Each line adds one more deposit to what came before, so the figure beside a line depends on the lines above it, and reading the statement from the bottom up would give different numbers.

The totals in the last lesson covered a whole group at once. A statement needs a total that grows down the page, and it invites a second kind of comparison too, between a line and its neighbours, such as how much more a deposit was than the one before. This final lesson adds both to the window.

intro.promise: By the end you'll add up the rows so far, and look at the rows just before and after.

recap.keyIdea: A frame decides which rows a window value adds, and LAG and LEAD read the neighbours in the stated order. A NULL there can mean no neighbour or no value.

blocks.text: You reached a balance of 90, then a running total of 180 at order 103. LAG gave 80 at order 104 and LEAD gave 40 at order 103.

recap.nextHook: You have now taken a table from rows to a finished report. Each lesson added one more thing a query can do, and the reports you write next will use them together.

questions.prompt: A shop keeps two tables, customers and orders. Which of them has one row for each order?
hints: Each table's id column names the thing its rows stand for. What do the ids in each table name?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The orders table has one row per order, identified by its order id. One customer can be associated with several of these order rows.

questions.onCorrect: orders. Its ids 101 to 106 name orders, so each row is one order, not one person.

misconceptions.feedback: That table holds one row per person. Look at which table's ids are the order numbers.

questions.prompt: How many rows of orders have customer_id = 1?
hints: Read customer_id, not the order's own id.
Look down the customer_id column for the value 1.
Count every row of orders that holds 1 in that column, and remember that one customer can have several.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 101 and 102 reference customer 1; there are two.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Count rows by what customer_id holds. One customer can appear on several order rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts Ada once, as in customers. Count the order rows that point at her.

questions.prompt: The amount for order 106 is unknown. Which value records that in the table?
hints: Unknown and known to be zero make different claims.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: NULL records a missing or unknown value. It does not mean an amount of zero or the text 'NULL'.

questions.onCorrect: NULL says the amount is missing. A 0 would claim the order was free, which is a different fact.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero is a known amount: it says the order cost nothing. Unknown is a different claim.
The orders table is not empty. Only one cell is missing.

questions.prompt: A shop's customers table holds Ada, Ben, Cy and Dee. Elm signs up and hasn't ordered anything yet. How many rows does customers hold now?
hints: Which table gets a row when a customer signs up?
Start from the customers already in the table.
Add the new customer to the four already there.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four original customers plus Elm make five customer rows.

questions.onCorrect: 5. A new customer adds a row to customers only. Orders stay as they were.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count before Elm joined. A new customer adds a row.

questions.prompt: Three customers each place two orders. How many rows should a one-row-per-order table have?
hints: Count orders rather than people.
Multiply the number of people by the orders per person.
Evaluate 3 × 2; each customer contributes two order rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three customers times two orders each makes six order rows.

questions.onCorrect: 6. One row per order: three customers with two orders each give 3 × 2 rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the customers. The table has a row for each order.
That adds 3 + 2. Each of the three customers contributes two rows, so multiply.

questions.prompt: Which column can repeat without making an order id ambiguous?
hints: Several orders can refer to the same customer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: orders.customer_id can repeat because one customer can place several orders. The separate order id still identifies each order uniquely.

questions.onCorrect: orders.customer_id can repeat. The order id stays unique, so each order is still named exactly once.

misconceptions.feedback: A primary key is different in every row, so it cannot repeat.
One of them can repeat: the one that points at a customer.

questions.prompt: How many columns does SELECT id, amount FROM orders return?
hints: Count the names in the list after SELECT.
Rows and columns measure different things, and this question asks about columns.
The list is id, amount. Count each name once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The SELECT list names id and amount: two columns.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each name in the SELECT list is one column of the result. The rows are unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every column of the table. The list names only some of them.
The list has two names, separated by a comma.

questions.prompt: A query contains amount AS price. What does the AS part change?
hints: An alias belongs to the result.

acceptedIdeas: The heading in the query result
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: AS price labels the column in this query's result. It does not rename the stored amount column.

choices.label: The heading in the query result

questions.onCorrect: The heading in the result. The alias labels the output and leaves the stored column alone.

misconceptions.feedback: The stored values stay as they were. AS only affects how the result is labelled.
Aliases never add or remove rows. They only label a column.

questions.prompt: A query works out amount * 2 for every order. What does it give for order 101, whose amount is 80?
hints: Apply the expression to this one row's amount.
Multiply 80 by two.
Evaluate 80 × 2. The alias, if there is one, only names the column.
questions.onCorrect: 160. The expression is worked out for each row; AS only names the new column.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2. The expression multiplies by 2.
That is the stored amount. The expression changes the value in the result.

questions.prompt: A query works out amount + 10 for every order. What does it give for order 102, whose amount is 20?
hints: This expression adds a fixed amount.
Add ten to twenty.
Evaluate 20 + 10; multiplication is not part of this expression.
questions.onCorrect: 30. This expression adds a fixed amount to each row, so a different question gets a different answer.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the amount. This expression adds 10.

questions.prompt: An amount is 15. What would SELECT amount * 3 AS tripled return for that row?
hints: AS names the column; the multiplication produces the value.
Multiply fifteen by three.
Evaluate 15 × 3, keeping the alias separate from the value.
questions.onCorrect: 45. Multiply 15 by 3; the alias tripled is only the heading.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 3. The expression multiplies by 3.
That is the amount before the expression is applied.

questions.prompt: After SELECT amount AS price, type the column name that remains in the stored table.
hints: SELECT reads the table; this alias does not alter its schema.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The stored column remains amount. The alias price belongs to the query result, so another query can still refer to amount.

questions.onCorrect: amount. The alias exists only in the result, so another query can still use the stored name.

misconceptions.feedback: price is the heading in this query's result. The table itself was never renamed.

questions.prompt: How many orders satisfy amount >= 40?
hints: Which amounts are 40 or more?
A comparison with an unknown amount is never true.
Go down the amount column and count each known amount that is 40 or higher. An amount of exactly 40 counts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 101, 103 and 104 satisfy the comparison; 106 has a missing amount.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The comparison keeps amounts of 40 and above, boundary included. The unknown amount never passes.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the boundary. At least 40 includes an amount of exactly 40.
One amount is unknown. A comparison with an unknown amount is never true.

questions.prompt: How many orders satisfy status = 'paid' AND amount >= 40?
hints: A row has to pass both tests, the one on status and the one on amount.
List the paid orders first, then check each of them against the amount test.
Cross out any paid order with an amount below 40.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only paid orders 101 and 103 also have amount at least 40.

questions.onCorrect: 2. AND needs both tests to pass, so only paid orders of at least 40 remain.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the status test. Every row must also be paid.
That is what OR would give. Here a row has to pass both tests.

questions.prompt: Which values can pass amount BETWEEN 20 AND 40?
hints: BETWEEN includes its two boundaries.

acceptedIdeas: Values from 20 through 40, including both ends
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: BETWEEN includes both endpoints, so 20 and 40 pass as well as values between them. An unknown amount does not pass this comparison.

choices.label: Values from 20 through 40, including both ends

questions.onCorrect: The range includes both ends. BETWEEN 20 AND 40 keeps 20, 40 and everything between.

misconceptions.feedback: Look at the two end values. Does BETWEEN keep a row at exactly 20?
There is also an upper end. Values above it fail.

questions.prompt: How many orders have item IN ('Book', 'Lamp')?
hints: An item can match either value in the list.
An unknown amount doesn't stop an item from matching.
Count the Book orders and the Lamp orders separately, then add the two counts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two Book orders and two Lamp orders make four.

questions.onCorrect: 4. IN accepts any value in its list, so two Book rows and two Lamp rows pass.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one of the two names only. A row passes if its item is either one.
That is every order. Only rows whose item is in the list pass.

questions.prompt: How many orders satisfy amount > 20 AND amount < 80?
hints: Both inequalities are strict.
Count known amounts strictly between the boundaries.
The known amounts are 80, 20, 80, 40 and 20. Keep only strict interior values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only order 104 has amount 40; the 20 and 80 boundaries are excluded.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Both comparisons are strict, so the amounts 20 and 80 are out and only 40 stays.

misconceptions.feedback: Strict comparisons drop the amounts exactly on the lines.
Check the amounts again. Which known ones sit strictly between the lines?

questions.prompt: Which condition finds an unknown amount?
hints: SQL provides a missing-value predicate.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use amount IS NULL to test for a missing value. Equality to NULL does not evaluate to true in SQL.

questions.onCorrect: amount IS NULL. Nothing equals NULL, so an unknown amount needs its own test.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing equals NULL, not even NULL. That test is never true.
Zero is a known amount. An unknown amount is a different state.

questions.prompt: A query returns the shop's orders. Which part of it promises that they arrive in increasing order of id?
hints: Ordering must be part of the query.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ORDER BY id ASC explicitly requests increasing ids. Without ORDER BY, the query makes no promise about the order of its result rows.

questions.onCorrect: ORDER BY id ASC. A query promises an order only when it asks for one.

misconceptions.feedback: How rows are stored is not part of what a query promises.
SELECT chooses columns. It does not choose a row order.

questions.prompt: With ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC over known amounts, which id appears first?
hints: Compare amounts before ids.
Which amount is largest, and how many orders share it?
The ties are settled by id in increasing order. Which of the tied ids comes first?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The maximum amount is 80; the lower of its two order ids is 101.

questions.onCorrect: 101. Amounts compare first. The tie between two 80s goes to the lower id.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the winner when the higher id goes first. Check whether id is ASC or DESC.
That amount is not the largest. Compare amounts before ids.

questions.prompt: The known amounts in the orders table are 80, 20, 80, 40 and 20. Sorted largest first, what do the first three rows add up to?
hints: Take the three largest known amounts.
Two orders share the largest amount, so list the amounts from the top, one per row.
Add the first three amounts in that list.
questions.onCorrect: 200. LIMIT 3 keeps the first three rows of the order: 80, 80 and 40.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the two largest amounts only. The limit keeps one more row.
That takes four rows. The limit stops after the third.

questions.prompt: A query reads WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY amount ASC, id ASC LIMIT 2. Which set of orders does it return?
hints: Read the filter, direction and limit together.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: WHERE first keeps paid rows, ORDER BY amount ASC puts the smallest amounts first, and LIMIT 2 keeps the first two. id provides a stable order for ties.

choices.label: The first two rows stored on disk

questions.onCorrect: The two smallest paid orders. WHERE chooses the rows, then ASC and LIMIT 2 pick from them.

misconceptions.feedback: ASC runs from the smallest upwards, so this takes the other end.
WHERE and ORDER BY decide the rows, not how they are stored.

questions.prompt: How many rows can LIMIT 10 return when only four rows satisfy WHERE?
hints: LIMIT is an upper bound.
There are only four eligible rows.
Use the smaller of the eligible-row count and the limit; LIMIT adds no rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A limit does not create records; the result contains the four eligible rows.

questions.onCorrect: 4. LIMIT is a ceiling. It never adds rows that are not there.

misconceptions.feedback: LIMIT sets a ceiling, not a target. It cannot invent rows.

questions.prompt: Two rows tie on amount. How do you make their order deterministic?
hints: A unique secondary sort key separates the tied rows.

acceptedIdeas: Add a unique id as a tie-breaker
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add a unique id after amount in ORDER BY. It settles ties on amount so the same rows have a defined order.

choices.label: Add a unique id as a tie-breaker

questions.onCorrect: Add a unique id as a tie-breaker. A second sort column makes the order fully decided.

misconceptions.feedback: Without ORDER BY nothing about the order is promised.
LIMIT cuts a result. It does not sort one.

questions.prompt: How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders return?
hints: Collect the different customer ids.
Repeated references collapse into one result row.
Make a list of the customer ids with each one written once, then count that list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The distinct ids are 1, 2 and 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. DISTINCT keeps each customer id once, so repeated references collapse into one row.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every order. DISTINCT collapses repeated customer ids.

questions.prompt: In the orders table every order has its own id. Why does SELECT DISTINCT item, id still return every row?
hints: DISTINCT compares the entire selected row.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: DISTINCT compares the complete selected row. Even when item repeats, the unique id makes every item-and-id pair different.

questions.onCorrect: Each item and id pair is different. DISTINCT compares the whole row, and the ids differ.

misconceptions.feedback: DISTINCT works on text as on numbers. The columns you list decide the outcome.
Items repeat: Desk and Book appear more than once.

questions.prompt: The amount column of the orders holds 80, 20, 80, 40, 20 and NULL. What does COUNT(DISTINCT amount) return?
hints: Ignore missing values for this count.
Count the different known amounts, not the orders.
Write each known amount once, then count the entries in that list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known distinct amounts are 20, 40 and 80. COUNT does not include NULL.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Only the known amounts 20, 40 and 80 count, each once.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the unknown amount as a value. COUNT(DISTINCT amount) skips it.
That counts every known amount, repeats included.

questions.prompt: How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, status FROM orders return?
hints: List the statuses separately for each customer.
Compare the full two-column row.
Write each customer's statuses once, then count the different customer and status pairs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Customer 1 has paid; customer 2 has paid and pending; customer 3 has paid and pending. That makes five pairs.

questions.onCorrect: 5. DISTINCT compares the full customer and status pair, and customers 2 and 3 have both statuses.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts customers only. Status is part of the row too.
That counts every order. Some customer and status pairs repeat.

questions.prompt: A result column contains North, South, North and NULL. How many rows remain after SELECT DISTINCT?
hints: Remove repeated North only.
One NULL remains as a distinct result value.
The remaining values are North, South and NULL; count these result rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: North, South and NULL form three distinct result rows.

questions.onCorrect: 3. DISTINCT collapses the repeated North, and NULL stays as one result row.

misconceptions.feedback: NULL is not removed by DISTINCT. It stays as a result row.
North is repeated, so DISTINCT keeps it only once.

questions.prompt: What does DISTINCT change?
hints: SELECT reads; DISTINCT shapes its returned rows.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: DISTINCT removes duplicate selected rows from the query result. It does not delete rows from the stored table.

questions.onCorrect: Only the query result. DISTINCT shapes the rows returned and leaves the stored table alone.

misconceptions.feedback: DISTINCT reads the table and never alters it.
Keys belong to the table's definition. A query cannot change them.

questions.prompt: What does COUNT(amount) return for the shop's six orders?
hints: Count known values in the column.
COUNT(amount) excludes the NULL row.
Order 106 has no known amount; inspect the amounts on all the other orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five rows have a non-NULL amount; order 106 is missing.

questions.onCorrect: 5. COUNT(amount) counts the known amounts, so the unknown one is left out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows, which COUNT(*) gives. COUNT(amount) skips the unknown amount.

questions.prompt: What is AVG(amount) for the shop's six orders?
hints: Add only known amounts.
Use the count of known amounts as the denominator.
Evaluate 240 ÷ 5; NULL is outside this denominator.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known total is 240 across five known amounts: 240 ÷ 5 = 48.

questions.onCorrect: 48. SUM adds the known amounts, and AVG divides by how many there are.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by all six rows, as if the unknown amount were a zero.
That is the total. AVG divides it by the number of known amounts.

questions.prompt: What is MIN(amount) for pending orders?
hints: Filter to pending orders first.
Ignore the missing amount; do not replace it with zero.
The pending amounts are a known value on order 104 and NULL on order 106; only the known value participates.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Order 104 is the only pending order with a known amount; MIN is 40.

questions.onCorrect: 40. WHERE keeps the pending orders, and MIN ignores the unknown amount.

misconceptions.feedback: The unknown amount is not a zero. MIN ignores it.
That is the smallest amount over all orders. Filter to pending orders first.

questions.prompt: With no matching rows, type the value SUM(amount) returns in SQLite.
hints: No observed sum is different from a known zero sum.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: SQLite SUM(amount) returns NULL when there are no non-NULL input values, including an empty matching set. COUNT instead returns zero for an empty set.

questions.onCorrect: NULL. With no rows to add, SUM has no total to report, which is not the same as zero.

misconceptions.feedback: A total of zero would claim that rows were added up. With no rows there is no total.

questions.prompt: Known values are 10 and 30, with one NULL. What does AVG(value) return?
hints: The missing value does not add to the count.
Divide the known total by two.
Evaluate (10 + 30) ÷ 2; the missing observation is excluded.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: AVG uses the two known values: (10 + 30) ÷ 2 = 20.

questions.onCorrect: 20. The unknown value is out of the sum and the count, so it is 40 ÷ 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by three, counting the unknown value. AVG leaves it out.
That is the total. AVG divides it by the number of known values.

questions.prompt: What changes when you use AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0))?
hints: The replacement becomes an input value to AVG.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: COALESCE replaces each missing amount with zero before averaging. Those rows now contribute to the denominator, which can change the average.

questions.onCorrect: Missing amounts count as zeros. COALESCE replaces NULL before AVG sees it, so the count rises.

misconceptions.feedback: COALESCE fills the gap before AVG runs, so the gaps no longer disappear.
The values AVG reads change as well, so the average can change.

questions.prompt: How many result rows does GROUP BY item produce?
hints: Identify different item names.
One result row represents one item group.
The groups are Book, Desk and Lamp; each gets a result row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are three item groups: Book, Desk and Lamp.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Each different item becomes one result row, so the rows now stand for items.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one row per order. GROUP BY gathers orders that share an item.
That counts the statuses. Count the different item names.

questions.prompt: Group the orders by item. Within the Lamp group, what is COUNT(amount)?
hints: COUNT(column) counts known values.
Compare the two Lamp amount cells.
In the Lamp group, order 104 has an amount and order 106 has NULL. Count only the known cell.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only order 104 has a known Lamp amount; order 106 is NULL.

questions.onCorrect: 1. COUNT(amount) counts only the known amounts inside the group.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts both Lamp rows. COUNT(amount) skips the unknown amount.

questions.prompt: Name the SQL clause that can filter groups on SUM(amount).
hints: The total exists after the rows are grouped.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can test SUM(amount). WHERE filters the input rows before their group totals are computed.

questions.onCorrect: HAVING. A group total exists only after grouping, and HAVING tests groups.

misconceptions.feedback: WHERE sees single rows before they are grouped, so the total does not exist yet.
GROUP BY makes the groups. Something else has to test their totals.

questions.prompt: Group the orders by item after WHERE status = 'paid'. What is the Desk group's SUM(amount)?
hints: Keep only paid Desk orders.
Add the two eligible amounts.
Evaluate 80 + 80 for the eligible Desk orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Paid Desk orders 101 and 103 have amounts 80 and 80; their total is 160.

questions.onCorrect: 160. WHERE keeps the paid rows, then the Desk group adds its two amounts.

misconceptions.feedback: Both paid Desk orders count. Add them.
That is the total of all paid orders. The question is about Desk only.

questions.prompt: How many item groups survive HAVING SUM(amount) >= 40 in the original data?
hints: Compute each group total first.
The threshold includes totals equal to forty.
The totals are Book 40, Desk 160 and Lamp 40; test each with >= 40.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Book is 40, Desk is 160 and Lamp is 40. All three meet the inclusive threshold.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Each group total is tested, and totals equal to the threshold pass.

misconceptions.feedback: Totals equal to the threshold pass, because >= keeps them.
Several groups reach the threshold exactly, and >= keeps those.

questions.prompt: What does WHERE status = 'paid' change in a grouped query?
hints: WHERE defines the rows supplied to the groups.

acceptedIdeas: It filters individual rows before grouping
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: WHERE retains only paid input rows before grouping. Group counts and totals are calculated from that filtered set.

choices.label: It filters individual rows before grouping

questions.onCorrect: It filters individual rows before grouping. The groups are built from what remains.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a job for a later clause. WHERE acts before any totals exist.
WHERE never renames anything. It keeps or drops rows.

questions.prompt: How many rows does the INNER JOIN of customers and orders on customer_id return?
hints: Count matches, not different names.
Ada, Ben and Cy each contribute two order matches.
Ada, Ben and Cy each have two matches; Dee contributes none to an inner join.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the six orders references one existing customer, so there are six matching pairs.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Ada, Ben and Cy each have two matching orders. Dee has none, so no pair holds her.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the different names. Count matching pairs instead.
That pairs every customer with every order. A join on the key pairs only matches.

questions.prompt: Why is Dee absent from the INNER JOIN result?
hints: An inner join requires a match.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An INNER JOIN retains only matching pairs. Dee has no matching order in this dataset, so her customer row contributes no result row.

choices.label: INNER JOIN keeps only the first customer

questions.onCorrect: She has no matching order. An inner join keeps only pairs that match.

misconceptions.feedback: Names do not affect matching. The key values do.
INNER JOIN keeps every pair that matches, not just one customer.

questions.prompt: How many pairs does CROSS JOIN produce for four customers and six orders?
hints: For each customer, include every order.
Multiply the table sizes.
Evaluate 4 × 6 for every possible customer-order pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every customer pairs with every order: 4 × 6 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: 24. A cross join pairs every customer with every order: 4 × 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two table sizes. A cross join pairs each row with every row of the other table.
That is the number of matching pairs. A cross join pairs every customer with every order.

questions.prompt: Which condition follows the stored relationship between orders and customers?
hints: The order's customer_id refers to the customer's id.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: c.id = o.customer_id follows the customer reference stored on each order. Matching the two tables' unrelated id columns would connect the wrong records.

questions.onCorrect: c.id = o.customer_id. The order's customer_id holds the customer's key.

misconceptions.feedback: That compares a customer key with an order key. They are different things.
A name is not a stored reference to an item.

questions.prompt: Customers A, B and C have two, zero and one orders respectively. How many rows does their INNER JOIN return?
hints: An unmatched customer contributes no inner-join row.
Add the order matches.
Evaluate 2 + 0 + 1; each matching order contributes a row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The matching pairs total 2 + 0 + 1 = 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Each matching order is one row, and the customer with none adds nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts customers with orders. Each matching order is a row.

questions.prompt: Why can a customer's name repeat in a correctly joined result?
hints: A one-to-many relationship creates one row for each match.

acceptedIdeas: A person can match several orders
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each matching customer-and-order pair produces a result row. A customer with several orders appears several times without the join being wrong.

choices.label: A person can match several orders
JOIN always duplicates every row twice
Names cannot be selected in SQL

questions.onCorrect: A person can match several orders. Each match gives its own row, so the name repeats.

misconceptions.feedback: Rows repeat once per match, and that number depends on the data.
Names are columns like any other and can be selected.

questions.prompt: How many rows does customers LEFT JOIN orders return?
hints: Keep each order match.
Add one row for the customer with no match.
Add Dee's preserved unmatched row to the six order matches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six matched order rows plus Dee's unmatched customer row make seven.

questions.onCorrect: 7. Six order matches stay, and Dee adds one preserved row.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the matches alone. Dee still has to appear.

questions.prompt: For Dee after the LEFT JOIN, what does COUNT(o.id) return?
hints: COUNT(column) ignores NULL.
The retained customer row has a NULL order id.
Dee's order id is NULL; COUNT(o.id) counts only non-NULL matched keys.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Dee has no matched order id, so COUNT(o.id) is zero.

questions.onCorrect: 0. COUNT of a column skips NULL, and Dee's order id is NULL.

misconceptions.feedback: COUNT(*) would count her kept row. COUNT of a column skips NULL.

questions.prompt: Where should o.status = 'paid' go if every customer must remain?
hints: Preserve the customer while restricting which orders match.

acceptedIdeas: In ON as a matching condition
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Put the paid condition in ON to limit which orders match while preserving every left-side customer. A WHERE test on the right-side status would remove unmatched customer rows.

choices.label: In ON as a matching condition
In WHERE as the only row filter

questions.onCorrect: In ON as a matching condition. That limits which orders match and keeps every customer.

misconceptions.feedback: Dee's order columns are NULL, so a test after the join drops her row.
An alias names a column. It cannot filter rows.

questions.prompt: Which predicate identifies customers with no matched order?
hints: An actual order can have a missing amount.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The joined order id is NULL when no order matched. Because stored order ids are non-NULL, o.id IS NULL identifies those unmatched rows.

questions.onCorrect: o.id IS NULL. The order key is filled on every real match, so NULL means none matched.

It changes the stored table names

questions.prompt: Which requirement applies to the SELECT results combined by UNION?
